items.stem: If prophylaxis is indicated, which antibiotic is commonly prescribed as a daily low dose to prevent recurrent cystitis?
items.rationale: Continuous prophylaxis for 6 months to 2 years commonly uses trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 40/200 mg, nitrofurantoin 50 or 100 mg, or cephalexin 125 to 250 mg once a day, or fosfomycin 3 g every 10 days. Fluoroquinolones are effective but not usually recommended because resistance is increasing, and nitrofurantoin is avoided when creatinine clearance is below 60 mL/min.
expl: Fluoroquinolones such as ciprofloxacin are not usually recommended because resistance is increasing.
Metronidazole is not active against the usual urinary pathogens.
Amoxicillin is not among the agents listed for prophylaxis of recurrent cystitis.

items.stem: Which is an important surface virulence factor of uropathogenic Escherichia coli?
items.rationale: P fimbriae (P or Pap pili) are surface adhesins that bind the digalactoside of the P blood group antigen on uroepithelial cells; they are the second most common virulence factor of uropathogenic E. coli and are important in ascending infection and pyelonephritis. Aerobactin and enterobactin are siderophores that scavenge iron, and alpha-hemolysin is a secreted toxin.
expl: Aerobactin is a siderophore, a small iron-chelating molecule rather than a surface structure.
Alpha-hemolysin is a secreted toxin associated with renal damage.
Enterobactin is also a siderophore used for iron uptake.

items.stem: A 35-year-old man has intermittent episodes of colicky right flank pain radiating to the groin, with tea-colored urine. He has had several urinary tract infections treated with antibiotics but now has no dysuria, frequency, or fever. Urinalysis shows many red cells, and creatinine is normal. Which test should be done next?
options: Noncontrast CT of the urinary tract
items.rationale: Recurrent colicky flank pain with hematuria suggests urinary calculi, and the diagnosis rests on imaging; patients with suspected colic need urinalysis and usually an imaging study, and noncontrast CT is the preferred first study because it shows the stone, its location, and any obstruction. Recurrent infections raise the possibility of struvite stones from urea-splitting bacteria, so stone composition and culture-guided antibiotics follow once a stone is found.
expl: Serum uric acid belongs to the later metabolic evaluation, not the first test.
A urine culture guides antibiotics when infection is present but does not show a stone; he has no current urinary symptoms.
Prostate-specific antigen has no role in evaluating flank pain in a 35-year-old man.

items.subject: Internal Medicine
items.stem: A 58-year-old man with knee osteoarthritis has had epigastric pain for 1 week and one episode of coffee-ground vomiting. He has taken ibuprofen 800 mg three times a day for 3 weeks, does not drink alcohol, and is not critically ill. Endoscopy shows multiple superficial gastric erosions without ulcer. What is the most likely cause?
items.rationale: Erosive gastritis is mucosal erosion from damaged mucosal defenses; it is typically acute and presents with bleeding, and its common causes are NSAIDs, alcohol, and stress. With high-dose ibuprofen, no alcohol, and no critical illness, NSAID injury is the likely cause; treatment removes the cause and adds acid suppression.
expl: Helicobacter pylori mainly causes nonerosive gastritis.
Autoimmune atrophic gastritis is a chronic disease that leads to vitamin B12 malabsorption.
Acute stress gastritis occurs in critically ill patients.

expl: Overt hypothyroidism has a low free T4.

items.rationale: Multiple sclerosis, a demyelinating disease, typically follows a relapsing-remitting course in which exacerbations alternate with remissions of partial or full recovery. Onset is usually between 20 and 40 years of age, women are affected somewhat more often, and paresthesias in one or more limbs are common.
expl: Tumors cause progressive deficits rather than remitting ones.
Transient ischemic attacks usually last less than 1 hour and are most common in middle-aged and older adults.
Nervous system infections cause an acute or subacute illness rather than a year of remitting episodes.

items.stem: Which is the most common infectious cause of focal, ring-enhancing brain lesions in people with advanced HIV infection?
items.rationale: Cerebral toxoplasmosis, usually with one or more ring-enhancing lesions, is the typical presentation of toxoplasmosis in HIV and one of the most common CNS infections in advanced HIV without prophylaxis; risk is greatest when the CD4 count is below 50 cells/µL. Primary CNS lymphoma also forms mass lesions but is a neoplasm associated with Epstein-Barr virus.
expl: Cytomegalovirus in HIV causes retinitis and disease of the gut, lungs, or central nervous system rather than ring-enhancing masses.
Primary CNS lymphoma is an Epstein-Barr virus–associated neoplasm, not an infection.
Cryptococcus spreads to the meninges and causes microscopic multifocal lesions rather than ring-enhancing masses.

items.stem: A 40-year-old woman is referred because her ALT is 3 times the upper limit of normal. She has no symptoms and no known liver disease. Serology shows HBsAg negative, anti-HBs negative, HBeAg negative, anti-HBe positive, IgM anti-HBc positive, and total anti-HBc positive. What is the interpretation?
options: Window period of acute hepatitis B
items.rationale: IgM anti-HBc is a sensitive marker of acute HBV infection and is occasionally the only marker of recent infection, reflecting a window between the disappearance of HBsAg and the appearance of anti-HBs. Chronic infection shows persistent HBsAg with predominantly IgG anti-HBc, and vaccination produces anti-HBs alone.
expl: Vaccination produces anti-HBs only, without anti-HBc.
Chronic hepatitis B requires persistent HBsAg, with IgG rather than IgM anti-HBc predominating.
An inactive carrier is HBsAg positive.

items.subject: Internal Medicine
items.stem: A 70-year-old woman with pneumonia was started on broad-spectrum antibiotics. Several days later she developed watery, nonbloody stools 5 to 6 times a day with abdominal pain. Which organism most likely causes her diarrhea?
items.rationale: Clostridioides difficile is the most common cause of antibiotic-associated colitis; antibiotic-induced changes in the gut flora are the dominant predisposing factor, and symptoms typically begin 5 to 10 days after antibiotics start. It should be suspected in any patient with new, persistent diarrhea within 2 months of antibiotic use or 72 hours of hospital admission.
expl: Giardiasis follows ingestion of contaminated water and causes prolonged, greasy diarrhea.
Vibrio parahaemolyticus follows ingestion of raw or undercooked seafood.
Nontyphoidal Salmonella follows contaminated food such as eggs or poultry.

items.subject: Internal Medicine
items.stem: A 30-year-old man has a reactive rapid plasma reagin (RPR) test at a routine examination. He has no signs or symptoms of syphilis. Which test confirms the diagnosis?
items.rationale: Latent syphilis has no clinical manifestations and is detected by serologic testing, which needs two kinds of test: a nontreponemal test (VDRL or RPR) and a treponemal test such as the T. pallidum particle agglutination (TP-PA) assay. A reactive nontreponemal test should always be confirmed with a treponemal test because nontreponemal results can be falsely positive. Darkfield examination needs lesion exudate, which latent syphilis lacks.
expl: Repeating a nontreponemal test does not exclude a false-positive result.
Darkfield microscopy examines exudate from a chancre or lymph node and has no role without lesions.
The VDRL is a nontreponemal test like the RPR and cannot confirm it.

items.subject: Internal Medicine
items.stem: Which statement about severe dengue is correct?
options: It is defined by severe plasma leakage, bleeding, or organ impairment
It is always accompanied by severe hemorrhage from the gut
It can be managed at home with daily outpatient follow-up
It needs transfusion whenever hematocrit rises and platelets fall
items.rationale: Severe dengue is defined by severe plasma leakage leading to shock or fluid accumulation with respiratory distress, severe bleeding, or severe organ impairment, so hemorrhage is only one route. All patients with severe dengue are admitted to a hospital with intensive care and blood transfusion. A rising hematocrit reflects plasma leakage; transfusion is given only for suspected or severe bleeding, signaled by a falling hematocrit, and prophylactic platelet transfusion in stable patients is not needed.
expl: Severe dengue may present with plasma leakage or organ impairment without severe bleeding.
All patients with severe dengue are admitted to a hospital with intensive care facilities.
A rising hematocrit reflects plasma leakage; transfusion is reserved for bleeding, signaled by a falling hematocrit.

items.stem: A 61-year-old man is admitted for abdominal swelling. Paracentesis shows a white cell count of 300/µL with 35% polymorphonuclear cells, ascitic albumin 1.2 g/dL, protein 2.0 g/dL, and triglycerides 320 mg/dL. Serum albumin is 2.6 g/dL. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.rationale: An ascitic triglyceride level above 200 mg/dL confirms chylous ascites, and SAAG values in chylous ascites vary with the cause. Here the SAAG is 1.4 g/dL (2.6 − 1.2), and the neutrophil count is about 105/µL (35% of 300), below the 250/µL threshold for spontaneous bacterial peritonitis. Chylous ascites is most common with lymphoma or lymphatic duct occlusion.
expl: Heart failure gives a high SAAG but does not explain a triglyceride level of 320 mg/dL.
Peritoneal tuberculosis gives a SAAG below 1.1 g/dL.
Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis requires an ascitic neutrophil count of 250/µL or more; here it is about 105/µL.

items.stem: A 45-year-old woman starts high-dose inhaled corticosteroid therapy for asthma. Which adverse effect should she be counseled about?
items.rationale: Local adverse effects of inhaled corticosteroids are dysphonia and oral candidiasis, reduced by using a spacer and rinsing the mouth after each dose. Systemic effects are dose related, occurring mainly above 800 mcg/day, and include adrenal suppression, osteoporosis, cataracts, skin atrophy, and easy bruising.
expl: Meningitis is not an adverse effect of inhaled corticosteroids.
Inhaled corticosteroids do not raise serum potassium.
Cardiac arrhythmias are adverse effects of theophylline, not of inhaled corticosteroids.

items.stem: A 55-year-old man with alcohol use disorder, bedridden after a stroke and with poor dentition, has had fever and foul-smelling sputum for 10 days. Chest radiograph shows an infiltrate in the posterior segment of the right upper lobe. Which organism group is the most likely cause?
items.rationale: Impaired consciousness from alcohol and dysphagia after a stroke are risk factors for aspiration, and periodontal disease adds anaerobic oral flora. Foul-smelling sputum, a subacute course, and involvement of a dependent segment such as the posterior upper lobe point to anaerobic infection.
expl: Staphylococcus aureus is a common cause of hospital-acquired pneumonia and can form pneumatoceles.
Haemophilus influenzae is a common cause of community-acquired pneumonia but does not cause foul sputum.
Moraxella catarrhalis mainly affects patients with chronic lung disease.

items.stem: A 35-year-old woman has 3 days of fever with chills and flank pain and now has vomiting, generalized weakness, and poor oral intake. Blood pressure is 100/70 mm Hg, heart rate 87/min, respiratory rate 19/min, and temperature 37.9 °C; her lips are dry, and she has costovertebral angle tenderness. She has no risk factors for multidrug-resistant organisms. What is the initial management of choice?
items.rationale: Oral outpatient treatment requires that the patient can take oral antibiotics and has no nausea, vomiting, volume depletion, or sepsis. With vomiting and dry mucosa she needs admission and parenteral therapy chosen by local susceptibility; without risk factors for multidrug-resistant organisms, options include an IV fluoroquinolone or a broad-spectrum cephalosporin such as ceftriaxone, with a switch to oral therapy after defervescence to complete 7 to 14 days.
expl: Piperacillin-tazobactam is kept for severe infection or risk of multidrug-resistant organisms.
Oral therapy is unsuitable while she is vomiting and volume depleted.
Ampicillin-sulbactam is not among the usual first-line choices for pyelonephritis.

items.stem: A sexually active 25-year-old man has a painless ulcer on the penile shaft that he noticed 2 weeks after unprotected sex. Examination shows a clean-based ulcer and bilateral nontender inguinal lymphadenopathy. Which treatment should be given?
options: Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM once

items.rationale: A painless, clean-based genital ulcer with nontender regional lymphadenopathy is typical of primary syphilis. CDC recommends benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM as a single dose for primary and secondary syphilis; additional doses do not improve efficacy.
expl: Three weekly injections are used for retreatment and for later stages of syphilis, not for primary syphilis.
Azithromycin 1 g orally once is a regimen for chancroid, which causes painful ulcers.
Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM once is the recommended regimen for uncomplicated gonorrhea.

items.rationale: Low-dose aspirin may decrease the risk of colorectal cancer, and the USPSTF has recommended it for primary prevention of cardiovascular disease and colorectal cancer in selected average-risk adults willing to take it for at least 10 years. items.subject: Internal Medicine
items.stem: Which feature helps distinguish osmotic from secretory diarrhea?
options: Secretory diarrhea has a small stool osmotic gap
Stool weight is higher in osmotic diarrhea
Osmotic diarrhea is often accompanied by bleeding
items.rationale: The stool osmotic gap, 290 − 2 × (stool sodium + stool potassium), separates the two: a gap below 50 mEq/L indicates secretory diarrhea, and a larger gap suggests osmotic diarrhea. Osmotic diarrhea is caused by unabsorbed solutes and stops with fasting, whereas in secretory diarrhea the bowel secretes more electrolytes and water than it absorbs, and diarrhea persists with fasting, often in large volumes.
expl: Secretory diarrhea persists with fasting; osmotic diarrhea stops.
Secretory diarrhea typically produces the larger stool volumes.
Bleeding suggests inflammatory diarrhea rather than an osmotic mechanism.

items.subject: Internal Medicine
items.stem: A 58-year-old man has 3 months of dyspepsia and nausea without reflux. Examination and laboratory results are normal. Endoscopy shows an inflamed stomach with a 5-mm ulcer on the lesser curvature; biopsies show no malignancy but are positive for Helicobacter pylori. What is the best treatment?
options: H. pylori eradication for 14 days and no further PPI
A lifelong proton pump inhibitor without eradication
H. pylori eradication for 14 days, then a PPI for 4 weeks
A lifelong H2-receptor antagonist without eradication
items.rationale: Ulcers associated with H. pylori require eradication of the organism and reduction of gastric acidity. Infected patients with a gastric or duodenal ulcer need acid suppression continued for at least 4 weeks, and eradication is confirmed by a urea breath test, stool antigen test, or endoscopy at least 4 weeks after therapy. Successful eradication lowers the 3-year recurrence rate to less than 10%.
expl: Stopping acid suppression after eradication leaves the infected ulcer with less than the 4 weeks of acid suppression it needs.
A lifelong PPI without eradication also leaves the infection and its risks in place.
Acid suppression without eradication leaves a recurrence rate above 50% and the gastric cancer risk of the infection.

items.subject: Internal Medicine
items.stem: Which laboratory finding is a direct marker of hepatocyte injury?
options: ALT twice the upper limit of normal
Direct bilirubin higher than indirect bilirubin
items.rationale: ALT and AST leak from damaged hepatocytes, so they are sensitive indicators of hepatocyte injury, and an elevated ALT is somewhat specific for liver injury. Bilirubin fractions reflect excretion, and albumin, globulins, and the prothrombin time or INR reflect synthetic function.
expl: A prolonged INR reflects synthetic function and can also result from vitamin K deficiency or warfarin.
Albumin and globulin levels reflect synthetic function and chronic disease rather than acute injury.
A predominantly direct (conjugated) hyperbilirubinemia points to impaired excretion or cholestasis.

items.stem: A 36-year-old man is admitted with acute pancreatitis. Within 24 hours his findings include a serum lipase 8 times the upper limit of normal, a BUN of 20 mg/dL, and new confusion with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 14. Which of his findings adds a point to the Bedside Index of Severity in Acute Pancreatitis (BISAP)?
items.rationale: BISAP gives 1 point each for BUN above 25 mg/dL, impaired mental status (Glasgow Coma Scale below 15), SIRS, age above 60 years, and pleural effusion on imaging. Only his confusion qualifies; lipase above 3 times normal supports the diagnosis of pancreatitis but does not grade severity.
expl: The BUN criterion is above 25 mg/dL.
The age criterion is above 60 years.
A lipase above 3 times normal is a diagnostic criterion, not a BISAP variable.

items.stem: A 62-year-old man is admitted for melena. Upper endoscopy shows a clean-based ulcer in the antrum. He is hemodynamically stable. What is the appropriate course of action?
options: Intermittent high-dose IV PPI and observe 1 to 2 days
Continuous PPI infusion at 8 mg/h and observe 3 days
Oral PPI and prepare for discharge
Low-dose IV PPI and observe 1 to 2 days
items.rationale: A clean-based ulcer (Forrest III) is a low-risk finding that does not warrant endoscopic therapy because the risk of rebleeding is low, and an oral daily PPI can be continued for ulcer treatment. High-dose IV PPI therapy is reserved for ulcers with high-risk stigmata such as active bleeding or a visible vessel.
expl: Intermittent high-dose IV PPI is also reserved for high-risk ulcers.
High-dose PPI infusion is for ulcers with high-risk stigmata.
IV therapy and longer observation add nothing for a low-risk, clean-based ulcer.

items.stem: A 20-year-old man has had recurrent abdominal pain with loose stools several times a week for 6 months, with no other symptoms; the pain is relieved by defecation. Complete blood count, blood chemistry, stool examination, thyroid function tests, and colonoscopy are normal. What is the diagnosis?
items.rationale: The Rome criteria require recurrent abdominal pain at least 1 day a week in the previous 3 months with two or more of: relation to defecation, change in stool frequency, or change in stool consistency. With no red flags such as rectal bleeding or weight loss and a normal evaluation, the diagnosis is irritable bowel syndrome, here diarrhea-predominant.
expl: Colon cancer is excluded by a normal colonoscopy and usually has red flags such as bleeding or weight loss.
Inflammatory bowel disease would show mucosal inflammation at colonoscopy.
Infectious diarrhea is usually acute and would be found on stool examination.

items.stem: Below what hemoglobin level (g/dL) is blood transfusion recommended for a patient with acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding and no cardiovascular disease?
items.rationale: A restrictive strategy is recommended: transfuse when hemoglobin falls below 7 g/dL, targeting 7 to 10 g/dL, because trials showed lower mortality and rebleeding than with a liberal threshold of 9 g/dL. For patients with cardiovascular disease or acute coronary syndrome, a threshold of 8 g/dL is advised.
expl: A threshold of 8 g/dL is advised for patients with cardiovascular disease.
A liberal threshold of 9 g/dL had worse outcomes than a restrictive one in trials.
Transfusing at 10 g/dL is unnecessary in a patient without comorbidity.

items.subject: Internal Medicine
items.stem: Excluding local anorectal causes, what is the most common cause of acute lower gastrointestinal bleeding in adults?
items.rationale: Diverticular bleeding is the most common cause of acute lower GI bleeding in adults (30% to 65% of cases). It presents as painless hematochezia, usually moderate to severe because the bleeding vessel is an arteriole, and most episodes stop spontaneously.
expl: Inflammatory bowel disease causes bloody diarrhea but is a less common cause of acute bleeding.
Colon cancer is a common cause of minor or occult bleeding in older adults.
Polyps may bleed but are a less common source of acute bleeding.

items.rationale: Platelets are given in active acute upper GI bleeding when the count is 50 × 10^9/L (50,000/mm3) or lower, as part of major hemorrhage protocols. High-quality data on platelet thresholds in GI bleeding are limited, and endoscopy can achieve hemostasis at counts below 50,000/µL.
expl: A threshold of 100,000/mm3 is higher than recommended.

A threshold of 75,000/mm3 is higher than recommended.

items.subject: Internal Medicine
items.stem: Which is a cause of anemia in chronic kidney disease?
items.rationale: Anemia of CKD is mainly due to decreased erythropoietin production, together with abnormal iron metabolism from chronic inflammation and a shortened red cell lifespan; uremia causes red cell deformity and hemolysis. Folate and vitamin B12 deficiency, bleeding from platelet dysfunction, and blood loss with hemodialysis also contribute.
expl: Folate and vitamin B12 deficiencies contribute, not vitamin B6 deficiency.
Erythropoietin production is decreased, not increased, in CKD.
Hypocalcemia is a feature of CKD but does not cause anemia.

items.stem: A patient has hypertension, weight gain, and proximal muscle weakness. Examination shows a moon face, central obesity, and dorsal and supraclavicular fat pads. What is the underlying condition?
items.rationale: Chronic excess cortisol causes facial rounding (moon face) with a plethoric appearance and truncal obesity with prominent supraclavicular and dorsal cervical fat pads (buffalo hump), along with hypertension and proximal muscle weakness.
expl: Obstructive sleep apnea accompanies obesity and hypertension but not cushingoid fat redistribution.
Pheochromocytoma causes episodic hypertension, headache, and sweating, often with weight loss.
Primary aldosteronism causes hypertension with hypokalemia, not cushingoid features.

items.stem: How should inhaled corticosteroids be used in a patient with stable COPD?
options: Added to a LABA and LAMA in selected patients
As monotherapy for initial maintenance treatment
Combined with theophylline as first-line therapy
items.rationale: Initial maintenance therapy for COPD is a long-acting bronchodilator (LABA or LAMA), escalating to LABA plus LAMA; an inhaled corticosteroid is added to both in selected patients, works best when blood eosinophils are at least 150/µL, and raises the risk of pneumonia. Inhaled corticosteroid monotherapy is not used.
expl: Exacerbations are treated with systemic glucocorticoids.
Inhaled corticosteroids alone are not a maintenance option; long-acting bronchodilators come first.
Theophylline is not recommended for stable COPD.

items.rationale: Aerobic training such as running is consistently effective for weight loss compared with no exercise, whereas resistance training such as weight lifting is not; head to head, aerobic training produced about 1 kg more weight and fat loss, probably because it expends more energy.
expl: Calisthenics are largely body-weight resistance exercise, which is less effective for weight loss than aerobic training.
Yoga expends less energy than aerobic training.
Weight lifting is resistance training, which has not been shown to reduce weight compared with no exercise.

items.rationale: Lymphoma often presents with mediastinal adenopathy and systemic symptoms such as fever and night sweats, and compression of the superior vena cava causes shortness of breath and facial edema. expl: Breast cancer is rare at 18 and does not usually present as a mediastinal mass with fever.
Lung cancer is rare in adolescents and young adults.
Thyroid cancer seldom causes superior vena cava obstruction at presentation.

Chest radiograph shows a right lower lobe opacity with air bronchograms. He is admitted to the ward and has no risk factors for MRSA or Pseudomonas. Which regimen is recommended?
items.rationale: For inpatients outside the ICU without MRSA or Pseudomonas risk factors, recommended regimens are a beta-lactam plus a macrolide, or an antipneumococcal fluoroquinolone alone. A fluoroquinolone is not paired with a beta-lactam for this indication, and clindamycin adds anaerobic coverage that is not needed.
expl: Clindamycin targets anaerobes and does not cover atypical pathogens.
Moxifloxacin, likewise, is used as monotherapy rather than combined with a beta-lactam.
A respiratory fluoroquinolone is used alone, not added to a beta-lactam, in this setting.

items.subject: Internal Medicine
items.stem: A 56-year-old man with diabetes has cough and difficulty of breathing. Chest examination shows bronchophony, egophony, and whispered pectoriloquy over the right lower chest. What do these findings indicate?
items.rationale: Bronchophony and whispered pectoriloquy occur when the voice is clearly transmitted through the chest wall, as with alveolar consolidation in pneumonia, and egophony also occurs with consolidation. Tactile fremitus is increased in consolidation and decreased in effusion and pneumothorax.
expl: Pneumothorax causes hyperresonance with absent fremitus and decreased breath sounds.
Pleural thickening produces the same dampened findings as an effusion.
Pleural effusion causes dullness with decreased breath sounds and absent fremitus; egophony may occur only at its upper border.

items.subject: Internal Medicine
items.stem: Which part of the lung is the primary site of disease in asthma?
items.rationale: Asthma is diffuse airway inflammation with partially or completely reversible bronchoconstriction, involving the bronchi and bronchioles; gas exchange is affected only secondarily, through uneven ventilation distal to narrowed airways.
expl: Pleural disease causes effusion or pneumothorax, not bronchoconstriction.
Interstitial lung diseases such as asbestosis involve the interstitium and cause restriction.
Destruction of alveolar walls characterizes emphysema.

items.stem: A 36-year-old man with a 9-pack-year smoking history has occasional shortness of breath and cough. Spirometry shows a pre-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC of 0.68 and FEV1 of 3.5 L (predicted 4.4 L); after a bronchodilator, FEV1/FVC is 0.90 and FEV1 is 4.6 L. What is the diagnosis?
items.rationale: The FEV1 rose by 1.1 L, 25% of the predicted value, which exceeds the 10% change that defines a positive bronchodilator response, and the post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC is normal. COPD requires persistent airflow limitation, with a post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC below 0.70.
expl: Chronic bronchitis is defined by chronic productive cough, not by reversible obstruction.
COPD needs a post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC below 0.70.
Pneumonia does not cause reversible airflow obstruction on spirometry.

items.subject: Internal Medicine
items.stem: A 66-year-old man has had chronic cough productive of copious phlegm, with intermittent blood-streaked sputum, for 2 years. Chest CT a month ago showed dilated bronchi in both lower lungs with cystic and cylindrical configurations. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.rationale: Bronchiectasis is dilation, thickening, and destruction of larger bronchi from chronic infection and inflammation; patients have chronic productive cough with intermittent exacerbations, and fragile bronchial arteries can cause hemoptysis. The diagnosis is made by imaging, usually CT.
expl: Asthma causes reversible airflow obstruction without permanent bronchial dilation.
Chronic bronchitis causes productive cough without dilated bronchi on CT.
Emphysema destroys alveolar walls and causes hyperinflation, not bronchial dilation.

items.stem: A 54-year-old man with chronic kidney disease and type 2 diabetes has easy fatigability and fever of 39.0 °C for 3 days. Chest ultrasound shows bilateral pleural effusions of about 500 mL each. Which finding is the indication for diagnostic thoracentesis?

expl: Fatigability does not by itself call for fluid analysis.

Bilateral, symmetric effusions without fever or chest pain may be managed without thoracentesis.

expl: GOLD 4 requires an FEV1 below 30% of predicted.

items.stem: A 64-year-old woman with cough and fever for 4 days is lethargic in the emergency department, with blood pressure 80/40 mm Hg, heart rate 132/min, temperature 39 °C, and respiratory rate 27/min. Which IV fluid should be given first?
items.rationale: IV fluid is the first-line intervention to restore perfusion in sepsis, and balanced isotonic crystalloid is preferred; about 1 L is given rapidly, and most patients need at least 30 mL/kg in the first 3 hours. Adding albumin to the initial bolus has shown little survival benefit.
expl: Albumin shows little survival benefit and is not the first fluid.
Hypotonic fluid shifts into cells and expands the circulation poorly.
Hypertonic saline is reserved for problems such as raised intracranial pressure or severe hyponatremia.

items.subject: Internal Medicine
items.stem: A 60-year-old man with a COPD exacerbation and pneumonia has an arterial blood gas showing pH 7.12, PaCO2 60 mm Hg, and HCO3− 19 mEq/L. What is the interpretation?
items.rationale: A PaCO2 of 60 mm Hg with acidemia is respiratory acidosis. In acute respiratory acidosis, HCO3− should rise 1 to 2 mEq/L for every 10 mm Hg rise in PaCO2, to about 26 to 28 mEq/L here; an HCO3− of 19 mEq/L is lower than expected, so a metabolic acidosis coexists, a mixed disorder.
expl: Respiratory acidosis alone would not lower HCO3− below normal.
Metabolic alkalosis would raise HCO3− above the expected level.
The raised PaCO2 shows a primary respiratory component.

items.subject: Internal Medicine
items.stem: An inmate has cough and fever, and other inmates in the same facility have similar symptoms. His chest radiograph shows fine reticular infiltrates. What is the most likely route by which his pneumonia was acquired?
items.rationale: Clustered respiratory illness in a crowded institution points to airborne spread. Tuberculosis, for example, is transmitted almost exclusively by inhalation of droplet nuclei, and transmission is enhanced by prolonged exposure in overcrowded, poorly ventilated, enclosed spaces such as correctional facilities.
expl: Direct inoculation follows penetrating trauma or procedures.

items.stem: A 47-year-old man with morbid obesity has been in two vehicle collisions in the past month and is evaluated for frequently falling asleep while driving. His STOP-BANG score is 7. Which test confirms the diagnosis?
items.rationale: Obstructive sleep apnea is suspected from risk factors and symptoms and confirmed by sleep studies; polysomnography, which records sleep stages and the occurrence and duration of apneas and hypopneas, is the gold standard for diagnosis and for grading severity. expl: Cranial CT does not evaluate breathing during sleep.

items.stem: Which pair of conditions is likely to produce similar physical findings on chest examination?
options: Massive effusion and diffuse pleural fibrosis
Pneumothorax and a large pleural effusion
items.rationale: A pleural effusion causes decreased breath sounds, dullness to percussion, and absent tactile fremitus, and pleural thickening (fibrosis) can cause the same findings. Pneumothorax also decreases breath sounds and fremitus but is hyperresonant, and consolidation increases fremitus and transmits the voice.

Bronchitis leaves fremitus and percussion normal, whereas consolidation causes dullness and bronchial breathing.
Pneumothorax is hyperresonant to percussion, whereas an effusion is dull.

items.stem: A 66-year-old woman is brought for anxiety, depression, and hallucinations. She also has a symmetric, scaly, hyperpigmented rash on the sun-exposed backs of her hands and neck, and chronic diarrhea. Which deficiency is most probable?
items.rationale: Niacin deficiency (pellagra) causes the 3 Ds: a pigmented, photosensitive rash (dermatitis), diarrhea, and neurologic and psychiatric changes leading to dementia. The rash favors sun-exposed skin, such as the backs of the hands and the neck.
expl: Iron deficiency causes microcytic anemia without a photosensitive rash.
Zinc deficiency causes a periorificial and acral dermatitis but not the neuropsychiatric syndrome of pellagra.
Folate deficiency causes megaloblastic anemia, not a photosensitive rash.

items.stem: Which subtype of acute myeloid leukemia has a good prognosis?

expl: AML with maturation is treated with standard intensive chemotherapy, with lower cure rates.
Acute monoblastic leukemia lacks a comparable targeted therapy and has a worse outlook.
Acute megakaryoblastic leukemia in adults carries a poor prognosis.

items.stem: In a patient with chronic myeloid leukemia on a tyrosine kinase inhibitor, which response is the treatment goal used to judge therapy?
options: A major molecular response in BCR::ABL
items.rationale: Response to tyrosine kinase inhibitors is measured at 3, 6, and 12 months with a molecular test (BCR::ABL) or a cytogenetic test (Philadelphia chromosome–positive cells); a major molecular response, BCR::ABL below one-thousandth of the expected untreated value, is the deeper target. Normal counts and regression of splenomegaly are only hematologic responses, and some patients with sustained deep responses can stop treatment and remain in remission.
expl: Normal blood counts define a hematologic response only.
Regression of splenomegaly is part of a hematologic response, the shallowest level.
Loss of Philadelphia chromosome–positive cells is a cytogenetic response, which precedes a molecular response.

items.stem: A woman with Hodgkin lymphoma has PET-avid lymph nodes in the inguinal, mediastinal, and supraclavicular regions, with no extranodal disease. She has lost weight and has drenching night sweats. What is her stage?
items.rationale: Nodal involvement on both sides of the diaphragm (inguinal below; mediastinal and supraclavicular above) without extranodal disease is stage III. Fever, night sweats, and unintentional weight loss of more than 10% in 6 months are B symptoms, so she is stage III-B.
expl: Stage IV-A would also require extranodal disease, without B symptoms.

Her night sweats and weight loss are B symptoms, so the designation is B, not A.

items.stem: A 35-year-old woman with aplastic anemia will receive a red cell transfusion. She had an urticarial reaction during a previous red cell transfusion. What should be done to prevent this reaction?
options: Nothing; such reactions are rare and will not recur
Give diphenhydramine and paracetamol as premedication
Irradiate the packed red cells before transfusion
items.rationale: Urticaria is a mild allergic reaction to components of donor plasma. In a patient with a previous allergic transfusion reaction, an antihistamine such as diphenhydramine 50 mg orally or IV may be given just before or at the start of the transfusion.
expl: Allergic reactions are common, and a prior reaction is a reason for prophylaxis.
Irradiation prevents transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease, not allergic reactions.
Leukoreduction reduces febrile nonhemolytic reactions, not urticaria.

items.stem: A 40-year-old woman is referred for a hemoglobin of 69 g/L. She is hemodynamically stable and has no complaints. Workup shows microcytic, hypochromic anemia due to iron deficiency. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Oral iron and evaluation for the cause
items.rationale: Uncomplicated iron deficiency without comorbidities is treated with oral iron, and hemoglobin should rise by at least 1 g/dL within 2 to 4 weeks. Once iron deficiency is diagnosed, occult blood loss should be suspected until proven otherwise, and its cause is treated. A stable, asymptomatic patient does not need transfusion.
expl: Washed red cells are for patients with severe allergic reactions or IgA deficiency, and she does not need transfusion.
Whole blood is not used to correct chronic anemia in a stable patient.
Transfusion is not needed in a stable, asymptomatic patient whose anemia will respond to iron.

items.rationale: Fanconi anemia, the most frequent genetic cause of bone marrow failure, carries a more than 500-fold incidence of head and neck squamous cell carcinoma compared with the general population.
expl: Lynch syndrome predisposes mainly to colorectal and endometrial cancers.
Li-Fraumeni syndrome predisposes mainly to sarcomas and breast, brain, and adrenal cancers.
Xeroderma pigmentosum predisposes mainly to skin cancers of sun-exposed areas.

items.stem: Aside from iron, deficiency of which B vitamins causes nutritional anemia?
items.rationale: Vitamin B12 and folate (B9) deficiencies cause megaloblastic anemia; the anemia of folate deficiency is indistinguishable from that of vitamin B12 deficiency, and B12 deficiency can also damage the spinal cord, brain, and peripheral nerves.

items.subject: Internal Medicine
items.stem: A 34-year-old woman with occasional joint pains is referred because her ANA by ELISA and her anti-RNP antibodies are positive. She has no current symptoms, and her examination, CBC, and urinalysis are normal. What is the most appropriate management?
items.rationale: A positive ANA occurs in many conditions and even in the general population, and anti-RNP antibodies alone do not establish mixed connective tissue disease; typical clinical findings are also required. Many patients first have an undifferentiated picture that may progress, so an asymptomatic patient with a normal CBC and urinalysis is followed for new features. Corticosteroids and other immunosuppressants are for moderate or severe disease.
expl: Corticosteroids are used for moderate or severe disease, not for positive serology without clinical disease.
Repeating the same assay adds no information and does not change management.
Immunosuppressants such as mycophenolate are reserved for moderate or severe disease.

items.subject: Internal Medicine
items.stem: An obese 25-year-old man is referred for preemployment clearance because a urinalysis showed glucosuria. He has no symptoms. What is the next step?
options: Reassure him that it is benign
Repeat the urinalysis in a week
items.rationale: Diabetes is confirmed by plasma glucose, for example a fasting plasma glucose of 126 mg/dL (7.0 mmol/L) or more, or by an HbA1c of 6.5% or more. Urine glucose is no longer used for diagnosis because it is neither sensitive nor specific. Glucosuria with normal plasma glucose is renal glucosuria, which is benign and needs no treatment, so blood glucose decides between the two.
expl: Reassurance is appropriate only after hyperglycemia is excluded, since glucosuria in an obese man may reflect diabetes.
Urine glucose is neither sensitive nor specific, so a repeat urinalysis cannot settle the diagnosis.
Treatment requires a diagnosis confirmed by plasma glucose or HbA1c.

items.stem: Which patient should be screened and treated for asymptomatic bacteriuria?
options: A man with bladder cancer who will start chemotherapy
A woman with diabetes and nonobstructing kidney stones
A woman with multiple sexual partners
A man scheduled for transurethral resection of the prostate
items.rationale: Screening for asymptomatic bacteriuria is limited to pregnant patients and to patients about to undergo invasive genitourinary procedures that can cause mucosal bleeding, such as transurethral resection of the prostate. expl: Starting chemotherapy is not an indication to screen for asymptomatic bacteriuria.
Asymptomatic bacteriuria is not treated in patients with diabetes, and nonobstructing stones do not change this.
Sexual activity is a risk factor for symptomatic infection but not an indication to screen.

items.stem: Which urinary sediment finding is most characteristic of glomerulonephritis?
items.rationale: Red cell casts and dysmorphic red cells indicate bleeding of glomerular origin and point to glomerulonephritis or vasculitis; the nephritic syndrome is defined by hematuria with dysmorphic red cells and often red cell casts.
expl: White cell casts indicate inflammation and are typical of pyelonephritis and interstitial nephritis.
Calcium phosphate crystals relate to stone formation, not glomerular injury.
Hyaline casts are nonspecific and accompany a normal sediment, as in prerenal azotemia.

items.rationale: Chronic kidney disease is classified by cause, GFR category (G1 to G5), and albuminuria category (A1 to A3). An eGFR of 45 to 59 mL/min/1.73 m² is category G3a, and an albumin-to-creatinine ratio of 30 to 299 mg/g is A2 (moderately increased), so the patient is G3aA2.

items.subject: Internal Medicine
items.stem: A 50-year-old man has recurrent kidney stones. His urine pH is 5.0, and urine microscopy shows uric acid crystals. Which drug is most useful to dissolve and prevent these stones?
items.rationale: Uric acid stones form in acidic urine (pH below 5.5). Raising the urine pH to 6 to 6.5, together with increased fluid intake, can dissolve them and prevents new ones. Potassium citrate is the preferred alkalinizing drug, and sodium or potassium bicarbonate is an alternative alkaline agent; among these options, sodium bicarbonate is the alkalinizing agent.
expl: Loop diuretics do not alkalinize the urine and are not used to treat uric acid stones.
Thiazides lower urine calcium and are used for calcium stones with hypercalciuria.
SGLT2 inhibitors are not a treatment for uric acid stones.

items.stem: Which complication should be anticipated during massive transfusion?
items.rationale: Rapid transfusion of large volumes of cold blood causes hypothermia, which can cause arrhythmias or cardiac arrest; blood is given through a warming device. Hypocalcemia, not hypercalcemia, can result, and dilution of platelets and clotting factors causes a dilutional coagulopathy.
expl: Citrate in stored blood binds calcium, so the risk is hypocalcemia.
Hyponatremia is not a recognized complication of massive transfusion.
Platelets are diluted, so counts fall rather than rise.

items.subject: Internal Medicine
items.stem: A 60-year-old woman with diabetes and chronic kidney disease has had anorexia, nausea, and vomiting for 1 month. Urine output is above 1 L/day. BP is 130/70 mmHg, heart rate 88 beats/min, respiratory rate 21 breaths/min, and BMI 18 kg/m². Hemoglobin is 88 g/L, sodium 135 mmol/L, potassium 4.8 mmol/L, creatinine 600 µmol/L, and bicarbonate 15 mmol/L. What is the treatment of choice for her symptoms?
options: Give an antiemetic and an appetite stimulant
items.rationale: Anorexia, nausea, vomiting, and weight loss are uremic symptoms, and dialysis is usually started at their onset; undernutrition with tissue wasting is a feature of chronic uremia. A creatinine of 600 µmol/L in a 60-year-old woman corresponds to an eGFR of about 6.5 mL/min/1.73 m² by the CKD-EPI 2021 equation, below the 15 mL/min at which these problems typically appear in patients with diabetes.
expl: Bicarbonate corrects the acidosis but not the uremia.
Anemia does not explain the anorexia, nausea, and vomiting, and transfusion does not treat uremia.
An antiemetic treats a symptom without treating the uremia that causes it.

items.stem: A 43-year-old man on maintenance hemodialysis for stage 5 chronic kidney disease has continuous, aching right thigh pain not relieved by NSAIDs. Serum calcium, phosphate, and PTH are high, and vitamin D levels are normal. What is the treatment of choice for his hyperparathyroidism?
items.rationale: Cinacalcet, an oral calcimimetic, resets the calcium-sensing receptor on parathyroid cells and lowers PTH in patients on dialysis without raising serum calcium, which suits a patient whose calcium is already high. Calcitriol and calcium-containing binders raise calcium, and sevelamer lowers phosphate without directly suppressing PTH.
expl: Sevelamer controls phosphate but does not directly lower PTH.
A calcium-containing binder adds calcium; non-calcium binders are preferred in hypercalcemia.
Calcitriol can raise calcium and phosphate, and his calcium is already high.

items.subject: Internal Medicine
items.stem: Which intervention slows progression of chronic kidney disease caused by diabetes?
options: A high-protein diet of 1.5 g/kg/day or more
An ACE inhibitor or ARB to reduce albuminuria
An HbA1c target of 9% to limit hypoglycemia
items.rationale: Angiotensin inhibition with an ACE inhibitor or ARB is first-line therapy: it lowers blood pressure and proteinuria, slows progression of diabetic nephropathy, and is started once albuminuria is detected. Other measures include an HbA1c of 7.0% or less, an SGLT2 inhibitor, and a protein intake of 0.8 to 1.2 g/kg/day.
expl: Beta-blockers are not the antiproteinuric drugs of choice; angiotensin inhibition is first-line.
The recommended protein intake in diabetic nephropathy is 0.8 to 1.2 g/kg/day, not a high-protein diet.
The HbA1c target is 7.0% or less.

items.subject: Internal Medicine
items.stem: A 55-year-old man with uncontrolled diabetes and polyuria is admitted with decreased sensorium. BP is 80/55 mmHg and heart rate 110 beats/min. Which best describes his extracellular fluid volume status?
items.rationale: Hyperglycemia causes an osmotic diuresis with large urinary losses of water and electrolytes. A loss of more than 10% of extracellular fluid volume is severe volume depletion and produces signs of shock such as tachycardia, hypotension, and confusion, all present here. Moderate depletion (5 to 10%) usually causes orthostatic changes, and mild depletion (under 5%) may show only reduced skin turgor.
expl: Mild depletion may cause only reduced skin turgor and thirst.
Polyuria from osmotic diuresis depletes, rather than expands, the extracellular volume.
Moderate depletion causes orthostatic tachycardia or hypotension, not shock with confusion.

items.subject: Internal Medicine
items.stem: In a patient with oliguric acute kidney injury, a fractional excretion of sodium below 1% most suggests which condition?
items.rationale: During volume depletion, normally functioning kidneys conserve sodium. In oliguric acute kidney injury, a fractional excretion of sodium below 1% points to a prerenal state such as hypovolemia, whereas a value above 2% points to acute tubular necrosis. The criteria do not apply after recent diuretic use.
expl: Acute tubular necrosis gives a fractional excretion of sodium above 2%.
In SIADH, the fractional excretion of sodium is above 1%.
Diuretics increase sodium excretion, and the criteria do not apply after recent diuretic use.

items.subject: Internal Medicine
items.stem: A 65-year-old man has serum sodium 150 mmol/L, blood glucose 6 mmol/L, and blood urea nitrogen 4 mmol/L. What is his calculated serum osmolality in mOsm/kg?
items.rationale: Calculated osmolality = 2 × sodium + glucose/18 + BUN/2.8 when glucose and BUN are in mg/dL; the divisors convert mg/dL to mmol/L. With values already in mmol/L, they are added directly: 2 × 150 + 6 + 4 = 310 mOsm/kg.
expl: 300 counts only twice the sodium and omits glucose and urea.
305 leaves out part of the glucose and urea contribution.
295 is less than twice the sodium alone.

items.subject: Internal Medicine
items.stem: Which medication can cause hyponatremia?
items.rationale: Thiazide diuretics are a common cause of hyponatremia: they impair the kidneys' diluting capacity and increase sodium excretion, and the resulting volume depletion triggers vasopressin release and water retention. The effect can last up to 2 weeks after the drug is stopped.
expl: Tolvaptan, a vasopressin V2 receptor antagonist, treats severe or resistant hyponatremia.
Sodium bicarbonate adds sodium and is not a cause of hyponatremia.
Demeclocycline is used to treat SIADH when water restriction fails.

items.subject: Internal Medicine
items.stem: Which diabetes medication is most associated with weight loss?
items.rationale: Empagliflozin is an SGLT2 inhibitor: blocking glucose reabsorption in the proximal tubule causes glycosuria, with modest weight loss and lower blood pressure. Sulfonylureas such as gliclazide and insulin cause weight gain, and DPP-4 inhibitors such as sitagliptin are weight-neutral.
expl: Sitagliptin is a DPP-4 inhibitor, which is weight-neutral.
Gliclazide is a sulfonylurea; sulfonylureas promote weight gain.
Weight gain is a common complication of insulin therapy in type 2 diabetes.

items.stem: A patient with palpitations and weight loss has a TSH of 0.1 mIU/L (reference 0.32 to 5) and a free T4 of 1.5 ng/dL (reference 0.8 to 1.8). What is the next diagnostic step?
items.rationale: In hyperthyroidism, some patients have only T3 elevated (T3 toxicosis). When TSH is low and free T4 is normal in a patient with symptoms of hyperthyroidism, serum T3 is measured; an elevated level confirms T3 toxicosis. Radioactive iodine uptake is used afterward to find the cause when it is not clinically evident.
expl: Radioactive iodine uptake identifies the cause once hyperthyroidism is confirmed and the cause is not clinically evident.
Serum thyroglobulin is measured when thyrotoxicosis factitia is suspected.
Ultrasound shows thyroid structure, not thyroid function.

items.stem: An asymptomatic 54-year-old woman has a fasting blood sugar of 129 mg/dL and an HbA1c of 5.6%. What is the next diagnostic step?
items.rationale: Without unequivocal hyperglycemia, diabetes requires two abnormal results. Her fasting glucose is in the diabetic range (126 mg/dL or more), while her HbA1c is normal (below 5.7%). When two different tests are discordant, the result above the diagnostic cut point is repeated, and the diagnosis rests on that confirmatory test.
expl: Waiting a year leaves a possible diagnosis of diabetes unconfirmed.
The HbA1c is already normal; the abnormal fasting glucose is the result to repeat.
A random glucose is diagnostic only at 200 mg/dL or more with symptoms, and she has none.

items.stem: An adult starting insulin uses a 4-mm pen needle. At what angle to the skin should the needle be inserted?
items.rationale: Children, adolescents, and adults should use a 4-mm needle with insulin pens, and these short needles are inserted at 90 degrees to the skin surface. A 45-degree angle is used with a 6-mm needle in children and lean patients.
expl: A 15-degree angle is used for intradermal injections, not subcutaneous insulin.
A 45-degree angle is used with 6-mm needles in children and lean patients.
A 30-degree angle is not recommended for insulin pen needles.

items.subject: Internal Medicine
items.stem: In hypothyroidism, water-binding glycosaminoglycans accumulate in the dermis and thicken the skin without pitting. What is this finding called?
items.rationale: Myxedema denotes severe hypothyroidism and, specifically, its skin changes: nonpitting edema and thickening of the skin and soft tissues, particularly of the face, hands, and legs.
expl: A positive Pemberton sign is facial congestion on raising the arms, from a goiter compressing the thoracic inlet.
Thyroid acropachy is subperiosteal new bone and swelling of the metacarpals in Graves disease.
Lymphedema is limb edema from lymphatic hypoplasia or obstruction.

items.subject: Internal Medicine
items.stem: A 41-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes takes metformin. Her HbA1c is 8.0%, she is gaining weight, and her BMI is 31 kg/m². Which drug is most appropriate to add?
items.rationale: In people with diabetes and obesity, drugs that promote weight loss, such as GLP-1 receptor agonists and SGLT2 inhibitors, are preferred. Thiazolidinediones such as pioglitazone commonly cause weight gain from fluid retention and added fat, sulfonylureas cause weight gain of 2 to 5 kg, and insulin also causes weight gain.
expl: Pioglitazone commonly causes weight gain, sometimes more than 10 kg.
Basal insulin causes weight gain and is not the next step for a modestly raised HbA1c.
Sulfonylureas promote weight gain of 2 to 5 kg.

items.subject: Internal Medicine
items.stem: Which thyroid cancer carries the poorest prognosis?
items.rationale: Anaplastic carcinoma is an undifferentiated cancer that accounts for about 1% of thyroid cancers but 20% of annual thyroid cancer deaths; it presents with rapid, painful enlargement. Papillary and follicular cancers have a 5-year overall survival of 98.4%, and long-term survival is common with sporadic medullary carcinoma.
expl: Most patients with sporadic medullary carcinoma survive long term.
Follicular carcinoma is a differentiated cancer with an excellent overall survival.
Papillary carcinoma is slow growing with an excellent overall survival.

items.stem: Which skeletal complication is characteristic of Cushing syndrome?
items.rationale: Excess cortisol causes osteoporosis, which can present with back pain, loss of height from vertebral collapse, and low-impact fragility fractures.

Paget disease of bone is accelerated, localized bone turnover unrelated to cortisol excess.
Osteophytes are a feature of osteoarthritis.

Moon facies describes the rounding of the face, not its color.

items.stem: Which physical finding best distinguishes Cushing syndrome from simple obesity?
items.rationale: Proximal muscle weakness, such as difficulty climbing stairs or rising from a low chair, is a more specific sign of hypercortisolism. Weight gain, a rounded face, and ordinary stretch marks also occur in obesity; striae suggest Cushing syndrome when they are wide (more than 1 cm), pigmented, and palpable.
expl: Ordinary stretch marks occur with obesity; only wide, pigmented striae point to Cushing syndrome.
A rounded face also occurs in obesity.
Weight gain in Cushing syndrome can resemble ordinary obesity, so BMI does not discriminate.

items.subject: Internal Medicine
items.stem: A patient with primary hypothyroidism started levothyroxine. After the TSH has normalized, how long can full relief of symptoms take?
items.rationale: TSH and T4 reach steady state about 6 weeks after a dose change, but symptoms improve more slowly; full relief can take 3 to 6 months after the TSH normalizes. Symptoms that remain unresolved despite biochemical euthyroidism call for a search for other diagnoses.
expl: Symptoms that persist this long with a normal TSH call for a search for another cause.
6 to 12 months overstates the usual lag.
1 to 2 months is about the time to biochemical steady state, before symptoms have fully resolved.

items.subject: Internal Medicine
items.stem: What is the usual full daily replacement dose of levothyroxine for an adult with no comorbidities and no residual thyroid function?
items.rationale: Patients with minimal endogenous thyroid function need about 1.6 to 1.8 µg/kg of actual body weight daily. Patients with heart disease start at low doses, such as 25 µg daily, with adjustment every 6 weeks.
expl: 1.0 µg/kg is below full replacement for an athyreotic adult.
1.2 µg/kg is below full replacement; lower doses suit older patients or those with heart disease.
2.2 µg/kg exceeds the usual adult requirement of 1.6 to 1.8 µg/kg.

items.subject: Internal Medicine
items.stem: A 57-year-old man with hypertension has had fever and a productive cough for 2 days. Temperature is 37.8 °C, heart rate 120 beats/min, respiratory rate 26 breaths/min, BP 80/50 mmHg, and SpO2 96% on room air. Chest x-ray shows right middle lobe consolidation and left paracardiac infiltrates. An IV line is in place. What is the initial management?
items.rationale: Hypotension from pneumonia with sepsis calls for IV fluids as the first-line intervention to restore perfusion, with at least 30 mL/kg of crystalloid within the first 3 hours, together with antimicrobials given immediately, ideally within 1 hour. Norepinephrine is the first-line vasopressor if hypotension persists after fluids. Oxygen is given as needed, and his saturation is normal.
expl: Oxygen is given as needed; his saturation is 96% on room air.
Norepinephrine is added when hypotension persists after fluid resuscitation.
An antipyretic does not treat the hypoperfusion.

items.subject: Internal Medicine
items.stem: A 70-year-old man in the ICU with sepsis, diabetes, and hypertension has minor bleeding at his urinary catheter, endotracheal tube, and nasogastric tube sites. Hemoglobin is 81 g/L, platelets 200 × 10⁹/L, PT 18.1 s (reference 10 to 12), aPTT 45 s (reference 29 to 33), and fibrinogen 2.5 g/L (reference 2 to 4). Which blood product is most appropriate?
items.rationale: Prolonged PT and aPTT with bleeding indicate a deficiency of several clotting factors, as in sepsis-associated DIC; fresh frozen plasma supplies all clotting factors. His fibrinogen and platelet count are normal, and his hemoglobin is above the usual restrictive transfusion trigger of 70 g/L.
expl: Cryoprecipitate is a fibrinogen source for hypofibrinogenemia with bleeding, and his fibrinogen is normal.
His hemoglobin of 81 g/L is above the usual restrictive trigger of 70 g/L.
Whole blood does not target his clotting factor deficiency and adds volume he does not need.

items.stem: Which IV fluid, given in large volumes, can cause hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis?
items.rationale: Rapid infusion of sodium chloride is a cause of normal anion gap (hyperchloremic) metabolic acidosis. This adverse effect of normal saline has led to interest in balanced, chloride-restrictive solutions such as lactated Ringer's and Plasma-Lyte.
expl: Lactated Ringer's is a balanced crystalloid that does not cause hyperchloremia.
5% dextrose in water contains no chloride.
Plasma-Lyte A is a balanced crystalloid with less chloride than saline.

options: Fecal occult blood testing begins at age 45
Fecal occult blood testing begins at age 50
Sigmoidoscopy alone is repeated every 10 years

Colonoscopy is repeated every 10 years in average-risk adults.

items.subject: Internal Medicine
items.stem: Which statement about the initial treatment of sepsis is correct?
options: Albumin is given to lower the fever
Blood cultures are drawn, ideally before antibiotics
Fluids are restricted to prevent pulmonary congestion
items.rationale: Routine cultures, including blood, are obtained before antimicrobials when this causes no substantial delay (under 45 minutes), so that empiric broad-spectrum therapy can later be switched to specific drugs based on culture and sensitivity results. IV fluids are the first-line intervention to restore perfusion.
expl: Albumin is used for volume in patients who received large crystalloid volumes, not to lower fever.
Initial therapy is broad-spectrum, narrowed once culture results return.
IV fluids are first-line; the aim is to restore perfusion without causing fluid overload, not to restrict fluids.

items.subject: Internal Medicine
items.stem: A 47-year-old man on postoperative day 3 after surgery for gangrenous cholecystitis develops sudden dyspnea and hypoxemia. Chest x-ray shows diffuse bilateral opacities without cardiomegaly, and echocardiography shows normal left ventricular function. The white cell count is raised with neutrophilia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.rationale: ARDS is defined by onset within 1 week of a known insult, bilateral opacities not explained by effusions, collapse, or nodules, and respiratory failure not fully explained by heart failure or fluid overload. Sepsis and pneumonia cause most cases; here the insult is an abdominal infection after surgery.
expl: Pneumonia usually causes focal opacities, whereas these are diffuse and bilateral.
Pulmonary embolism does not cause diffuse bilateral opacities.
Normal left ventricular function and no cardiomegaly argue against cardiogenic edema.

items.subject: Internal Medicine
items.stem: A 62-year-old woman has sepsis from pneumonia. BP is 110/60 mmHg, heart rate 121 beats/min, and respiratory rate 29 breaths/min. Arterial blood gas shows pH 6.90, bicarbonate 9 mmol/L, and PaCO2 18 mmHg; creatinine is 1.2 mg/dL and potassium 4.0 mmol/L. Which treatment is most appropriate for her metabolic acidosis?
items.rationale: Treatment of the cause is paramount in lactic acidosis, but most experts give IV bicarbonate for severe metabolic acidosis (pH below 7.0) because of the risk of cardiovascular instability at lower pH, aiming for a pH of at least 7.10. The 2021 Surviving Sepsis Campaign guideline suggests bicarbonate in septic shock when the pH is 7.2 or lower with acute kidney injury, and suggests against it when given only to improve hemodynamics in hypoperfusion-induced lactic acidemia.
expl: Hemodialysis is for acidosis that cannot otherwise be controlled; her creatinine and potassium are normal.
Fomepizole treats methanol or ethylene glycol poisoning, which nothing here suggests.
She is not hypotensive, and inotropes do not correct acidosis.

items.stem: Which patient should receive a platelet transfusion?
options: Acute leukemia on chemotherapy, no bleeding, platelets 6,000/µL

items.stem: What is expected during a severe acute systemic inflammatory response?
items.rationale: Inflammation, infection, and other catabolic states break down body protein faster than it is replaced, producing a net loss of protein (negative nitrogen balance). Metabolic stress from critical illness, infection, or inflammation raises the resting metabolic rate, though rarely by more than 50%.
expl: A positive balance reflects net protein gain, as during tissue building.
Resting energy expenditure falls in undernutrition, not in acute inflammation.
Metabolic stress raises the resting metabolic rate.

items.subject: Internal Medicine
items.stem: What is the fluid of choice for initial volume resuscitation in sepsis?
items.rationale: Crystalloids are the recommended first-line resuscitation fluid, and balanced crystalloids are suggested over normal saline. Albumin is suggested only for patients who have received large volumes of crystalloids, starches are associated with increased mortality and are not used, and hypotonic dextrose solutions are not used for resuscitation.
expl: Albumin is reserved for patients who have received large volumes of crystalloids.
Hydroxyethyl starch is associated with increased mortality and should not be used.
Hypotonic fluids such as 5% dextrose in water should not be used for resuscitation.

items.subject: Internal Medicine
items.stem: A severely malnourished 38-year-old woman has generalized dry skin with fine, bran-like scaling and patchy hair loss. Which deficiency is most likely?
items.rationale: Essential fatty acid deficiency causes a generalized, scaly dermatitis, alopecia, and thrombocytopenia; the dermatitis increases water loss from the skin. It can develop within 3 weeks of fat-free parenteral nutrition.
expl: Folate deficiency causes megaloblastic anemia, sometimes with glossitis and diarrhea.

options: A low-protein diet gives the most weight loss
Reduced calories matter more than the macronutrient mix
A low-carbohydrate diet gives the most weight loss

expl: Diets with 15% and 25% protein produced similar weight loss.
Diets with 65% and 35% carbohydrate produced similar weight loss.

items.stem: A woman with obesity is willing to diet but cannot exercise because of her schedule. How should she be advised about weight loss?
options: Diet and exercise together are required for any weight loss
Exercise alone is more effective than diet alone
Drug treatment is essential for successful weight loss
Diet alone, without exercise, can produce weight loss

items.rationale: Intermittent fasting falls into three broad strategies: time-restricted eating, alternate-day fasting, and whole-day fasting. Whole-day fasting, such as the 5:2 diet, did not reduce weight more than continuous calorie restriction.

items.stem: A 42-year-old woman who has followed a strict vegan diet for years without supplements has a sore, swollen tongue, numbness of both feet, and macrocytic anemia. Which vitamin deficiency is most likely?
items.rationale: Vitamin B12 deficiency can develop in vegans who do not take supplements and causes megaloblastic anemia, damage to the spinal cord and brain, and peripheral neuropathy; glossitis, felt as burning of the tongue, is uncommon. Folate deficiency also causes macrocytic anemia and glossitis, but folate is plentiful in plant foods.

Riboflavin deficiency causes glossitis and cheilosis with a normocytic anemia.

items.rationale: Albumin has a half-life of about 20 days, so serum levels take weeks to rise or fall, although changes can be rapid in critical illness. Shorter-lived proteins such as prealbumin, transferrin, and retinol-binding protein fall more quickly as undernutrition progresses.

30 to 45 days is longer than albumin's half-life of about 20 days.

expl: Neoadjuvant chemotherapy is used for selected invasive cancers, not DCIS.

items.rationale: Giant cell arteritis affects people over 50 (mean onset about 70 years) and involves the aorta, its large branches in the neck, and the extracranial carotid branches. Headache, constitutional symptoms, claudication of the jaw or limbs, and a high ESR are typical, and 40 to 60% of patients have symptoms of polymyalgia rheumatica. Takayasu arteritis causes similar pulse deficits but affects young women, mostly aged 15 to 30.
expl: Polymyalgia rheumatica alone does not cause pulse deficits or limb claudication.
Takayasu arteritis mostly affects women aged 15 to 30.
Behçet syndrome presents with recurrent oral and genital ulcers and uveitis.

items.stem: Which statement about the laboratory features of rheumatoid arthritis is correct?
options: RA can occur with negative RF and anti-CCP
RF and anti-CCP levels rise and fall with disease activity
RF and anti-CCP have diagnostic but no prognostic value
RF is more specific than anti-CCP
items.rationale: RF is present in about 70% of patients, and some patients have neither RF nor anti-CCP (seronegative rheumatoid arthritis); destructive arthritis can occur without these antibodies. Anti-CCP is highly specific (about 90%), whereas low-titer RF also occurs in other diseases and in 3% of the general population. Both antibodies predict a worse prognosis, and their levels do not fluctuate with disease activity.
expl: RF and anti-CCP levels do not fluctuate with disease activity.
Both antibodies predict a worse prognosis.
Anti-CCP is more specific; RF also occurs in other diseases and in healthy people.

items.rationale: Systemic sclerosis has 3 hallmarks: vascular injury with widespread microangiopathy, autoimmunity with autoantibodies in nearly all patients, and tissue fibrosis. Its vasculopathy is noninflammatory and proliferative or obliterative, so systemic vasculitis is not one of its cardinal processes.
expl: Vasculitis and amyloid deposition are not cardinal processes of systemic sclerosis.
Vasculitis and granulomas are not cardinal processes of systemic sclerosis.

items.stem: Drug treatment is indicated for triglyceride levels above 500 mg/dL mainly to reduce the risk of which complication?
items.rationale: Guidelines support lowering triglycerides above 500 mg/dL to reduce the risk of pancreatitis; fibrates are the drugs of choice when only triglycerides are elevated. Whether elevated triglycerides independently contribute to cardiovascular disease is unclear.
expl: Stroke prevention is not the reason for treating very high triglycerides.

Steatohepatitis is not the main reason for drug treatment at this level.

items.stem: A 33-year-old man has had poorly controlled hypertension for 6 months with hypokalemia. What is the appropriate screening test?
items.rationale: Primary aldosteronism is suspected in hypertension with hypokalemia, and initial testing is plasma aldosterone with plasma renin activity, ideally off drugs that affect the renin-angiotensin system. Saline infusion, oral salt loading, and fludrocortisone suppression are confirmatory tests done after an abnormal screen.
expl: Saline infusion confirms primary aldosteronism after a positive screen.
Oral sodium loading confirms primary aldosteronism after a positive screen.
Fludrocortisone suppression confirms primary aldosteronism after a positive screen.

items.stem: A patient on long-term parenteral nutrition infused over 12 hours each night develops cholestasis. The soybean-based lipid emulsion dose is 1.5 g/kg/day. Which change is most likely to help?
options: Limit soybean lipid emulsion to 1 g/kg/day
Stop all oral and enteral intake
items.rationale: Soybean-based lipid emulsion should not exceed 1 g/kg/day, because excess is linked to hepatic steatosis, inflammation, and intestinal failure-associated liver disease; switching to a fish oil-based emulsion can speed reversal of cholestasis. Cyclic infusion carries a lower risk of liver injury than continuous infusion, enteral intake supports bile flow, and high protein and carbohydrate doses are associated with liver disease.
expl: Cyclic infusion is associated with less liver injury than continuous infusion.
Lack of enteral intake reduces bile flow, so oral and enteral intake should continue.
High protein doses are associated with intestinal failure-associated liver disease.

items.stem: A 75-year-old man with hypertension and 3 months of poor oral intake has swollen, bleeding gums and loose teeth. Which vitamin is deficient?

expl: Vitamin B12 deficiency causes megaloblastic anemia and neurologic damage.
Vitamin A deficiency causes night blindness and xerophthalmia.
Vitamin D deficiency causes osteomalacia in adults.

items.stem: What is the recommended treatment for uncomplicated gonococcal urethritis in a man weighing 70 kg in whom chlamydial infection has been excluded?
options: Cefixime 800 mg orally as a single dose

Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM as a single dose
Azithromycin 2 g orally as a single dose

items.stem: A healthy 64-year-old man is found to have a hemoglobin of 21.3 g/dL (reference 13 to 16). He looks flushed and has occasional headaches. A JAK2 V617F mutation is detected, and serum erythropoietin is low. What is the appropriate therapy?
items.rationale: Phlebotomy is the mainstay of treatment for polycythemia vera, with targets of a hematocrit below 45% in men and below 42% in women; low-dose aspirin is added for microvascular symptoms. The JAK2 mutation and low erythropoietin identify polycythemia vera, a primary myeloproliferative neoplasm, rather than secondary erythrocytosis.
expl: Aspirin, not clopidogrel, is used for microvascular symptoms, and antiplatelet therapy does not lower the red cell mass.
IV hydration corrects relative erythrocytosis from dehydration, not a true increase in red cell mass.
Polycythemia vera is a primary marrow neoplasm with no secondary cause to correct.

expl: Mannitol is not given before the airway is secured.
IV access supports circulation, which follows airway and breathing.
CT confirms the injury after the patient is stabilized.

items.rationale: NICE advises vaginal micronized progesterone, 400 mg twice daily, for women with bleeding in a scan-confirmed intrauterine pregnancy who have had a previous miscarriage, continued to 16 completed weeks when a heartbeat is seen. items.rationale: Pregnancy is the most common cause of amenorrhea in women of reproductive age, and spotting with pelvic pain raises concern for ectopic pregnancy or miscarriage. A pregnancy test comes before any further evaluation, and its result directs the rest of the workup.

A complete blood count helps judge blood loss but does not identify the cause.

items.rationale: Breech presentation is favored by conditions that change the shape of the uterine cavity or limit fetal turning, including uterine abnormalities such as septate, bicornuate, and didelphys uterus.
expl: Young maternal age is not among the causes of breech presentation.

items.stem: During a vaginal delivery, the fetal head delivers and then retracts against the perineum. What is the first maneuver?

The Woods screw maneuver is a later internal rotation maneuver.

items.stem: Friedman divided labor functionally into a preparatory division, a dilatational division, and which third division?
items.rationale: Friedman described three divisions of labor: the preparatory division (now the latent phase), the dilatational division (the active phase), and the pelvic division, which corresponds to the second stage, when the fetus descends through the pelvis.
expl: Deceleration is a phase near the end of active cervical dilation on Friedman's curve, not one of the three divisions.
The latent phase is the modern name for the preparatory division named in the stem.
Acceleration is a phase at the start of active labor on Friedman's curve, not one of the three divisions.

items.subject: OB-GYN
items.stem: A 28-year-old primipara has just delivered a term baby and the placenta. The hour that follows falls within which period?
items.rationale: The puerperium is the 6-week period after delivery, so the hour after delivery falls within it. The time from delivery of the placenta to 4 hours postpartum is also called the fourth stage of labor, when most complications, especially hemorrhage, occur.
expl: Parturition is the process of giving birth, which ends with delivery of the placenta.
Prodromal labor is the period of irregular contractions before labor begins.
The latent phase is the early part of the first stage of labor.

items.rationale: A large, nodular mass in the fundus is the fetal breech, and a round part over the pubis is the head, so the fetal long axis is parallel to the mother's: a longitudinal lie with cephalic presentation. expl: With the breech in the fundus and the head over the pubis, the fetus is not lying obliquely.
An oblique lie sets the fetal axis at an angle, with neither pole squarely in the fundus and over the inlet.
In a transverse lie the fetal long axis is perpendicular to the mother's, so no pole lies in the fundus or over the pelvis.

items.stem: Clinical pelvimetry in a G1P0 at 37 weeks shows a diagonal conjugate of 12 cm, a curved sacrum, prominent ischial spines, an interspinous diameter of 9 cm, and an intertuberous diameter of 9 cm. How is her pelvis interpreted?
items.rationale: The interspinous distance, the narrowest space the head must pass, is normally about 10 cm, so 9 cm with prominent spines indicates a contracted midplane. The diagonal conjugate of 12 cm is close to the 12.5-cm average, and an intertuberous diameter of 9 cm lies within the usual 8 to 11 cm, so the inlet and outlet are adequate.

The interspinous diameter of 9 cm is below the usual 10 cm, so the pelvis is not normal.
An intertuberous diameter of 9 cm lies within the usual 8 to 11 cm, so the outlet is adequate.

items.stem: Which agent, given to women at high risk, has been shown to reduce severe preeclampsia and fetal growth restriction?
items.rationale: Meta-analyses show that low-dose aspirin in women with risk factors reduces severe preeclampsia and fetal growth restriction. Aspirin 81 mg/day is recommended for high-risk patients, started at 12 to 28 weeks (ideally before 16 weeks) and continued until delivery.
expl: Iron prevents or treats iron deficiency but does not prevent preeclampsia.
Vitamin E has not been shown to prevent preeclampsia.
Folic acid reduces the risk of neural tube defects but does not prevent preeclampsia.

items.subject: OB-GYN
items.stem: A G2P1 at 39 weeks has an ultrasound biophysical assessment scored 6/8 because fetal movements were not seen. Amniotic fluid volume is normal, and the nonstress test has not yet been done. What is the next step?
items.rationale: The biophysical profile has five components, including a reactive nonstress test, each scored 2 or 0. A score of 6/8 covers only the ultrasound components, so the nonstress test completes the profile: a total of 8 or 10 indicates fetal well-being, and 6/10 at 37 weeks or more is equivocal and favors delivery.
expl: Delivery is decided on the completed score, and 6/8 on ultrasound alone is not a final score.
Waiting a week leaves an incomplete and possibly equivocal profile unresolved.
Intravenous hydration does not address fetal status.

items.stem: A G2P1 has a prepregnancy body mass index of 22. What total weight gain is recommended for this pregnancy?
items.rationale: Weight-gain targets follow the Institute of Medicine guidelines by prepregnancy body mass index. For a normal-weight woman (body mass index 18.5 to 24.9), the recommended total gain is 11.5 to 16 kg (25 to 35 lb).
expl: 15 to 25 lb is the target for overweight women (body mass index 25 to 29.9).
11 to 20 lb is the target for women with obesity (body mass index 30 or more).
28 to 40 lb is the target for underweight women (body mass index under 18.5).

items.topic: Early pregnancy loss, ectopic pregnancy, and hyperemesis
items.stem: A 28-year-old G1P0 at 8 weeks has vomited for 3 days and cannot keep down food or fluids. Her eyes are sunken. She has no fever or abdominal pain, and her blood pressure is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.rationale: Hyperemesis gravidarum is severe nausea and vomiting in pregnancy that causes dehydration, weight loss, and ketosis, typically in the first trimester. Sunken eyes reflect the dehydration.
expl: Gastritis causes epigastric pain and is not the usual cause of intractable vomiting at 8 weeks of pregnancy.
Gestational hypertension begins after 20 weeks, and her blood pressure is normal.
Appendicitis causes abdominal pain and often fever, which she does not have.

items.stem: Which of the following is an acquired cause of anemia in pregnancy?
items.rationale: Iron deficiency and folate deficiency, both acquired, are the most common causes of nonphysiologic anemia in pregnancy. Thalassemia, sickle cell disease, and hereditary spherocytosis are inherited.
expl: Sickle cell disease is an inherited hemoglobinopathy.
Hereditary spherocytosis is an inherited red cell membrane disorder.
Beta-thalassemia is an inherited disorder of hemoglobin synthesis.

items.stem: A woman at 36 weeks reports leaking fluid. Which of the following can turn Nitrazine paper blue even when the membranes are intact?
items.rationale: Amniotic fluid is alkaline and turns Nitrazine paper blue, while normal vaginal fluid is acidic. Blood, semen, alkaline antiseptics, urine, and bacterial vaginosis can also raise the pH and give a false-positive result.
expl: Normal vaginal secretions are acidic and do not turn the paper blue.
Fluid is sampled from the posterior fornix for testing; the site itself does not cause a false result.
Prolonged leakage leaves little fluid to test and does not make the paper turn blue falsely.

items.stem: A 23-year-old with severe right lower quadrant pain undergoes laparotomy for suspected appendicitis. Purulent fluid is found in the paracolic gutters, both fallopian tubes are swollen and inflamed, and the appendix is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.rationale: Pelvic inflammatory disease is a polymicrobial infection of the upper genital tract. Salpingitis and endometritis tend to occur together, and severe infection spreads to the ovaries and peritoneum, producing purulent peritoneal fluid with swollen tubes.
expl: A normal appendix excludes appendicitis.
Pyelonephritis is a kidney infection and does not produce pus around the tubes.
A ruptured ectopic pregnancy produces blood in the peritoneum, not pus.
