items.subject: Pediatrics
items.stem: A 4-year-old is brought to the emergency room with inspiratory stridor and a brassy cough. A neck radiograph shows a steeple sign. Which drug is the treatment of choice?
items.rationale: Stridor, a brassy cough, and the steeple sign of subglottic narrowing indicate viral croup. Oral corticosteroids are well established in croup because they reduce edema of the laryngeal mucosa, and a single oral dose of dexamethasone is the regimen most studied.
expl: Croup is viral, so a macrolide antibiotic has no role.
Chloral hydrate is a sedative; sedation does not relieve the airway edema and can mask worsening obstruction.
Ceftriaxone treats bacterial airway infections such as epiglottitis or bacterial tracheitis, which this child does not have.

items.stem: A 10-month-old is seen in the outpatient clinic for fever and cough. Which finding most reliably suggests pneumonia?
items.rationale: Tachypnea is the most consistent clinical manifestation of pneumonia in children. The World Health Organization counts 50 breaths/min or more as fast breathing at 2 to 11 months, so a rate above 60/min in a 10-month-old is clearly fast.
expl: Cough also occurs with upper respiratory infections and bronchitis, so it does not distinguish pneumonia.
A temperature of 38°C is a nonspecific sign of infection.
A heart rate of 110/min is within the normal range for a 10-month-old.

items.subject: Pediatrics
items.stem: A child snores loudly most nights and breathes with effort during sleep, and his parents have seen pauses in his breathing. What is the most likely condition?
items.rationale: Obstructive sleep apnea is repeated, prolonged upper airway obstruction during sleep despite continued or increased respiratory effort. Its most common nighttime features are loud, frequent snoring, breathing pauses, and choking or gasping arousals.
expl: Central hypoventilation causes shallow breathing in sleep without the obstruction and increased effort that produce snoring.
Foreign body aspiration causes sudden choking, cough, or wheeze unrelated to sleep.
Croup is an acute viral illness with a barking cough and stridor; it does not cause habitual snoring with pauses in sleep.

items.stem: A 3-day-old infant has thick, purulent eye discharge and swollen eyelids. The infection progresses to involve the cornea. What is the most likely cause?
items.rationale: Conjunctivitis caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae usually begins 2-5 days after birth, and gonococcus and Pseudomonas are the organisms capable of causing corneal perforation, blindness, and death. Purulent discharge and lid swelling on day 3 with spread to the cornea fit gonococcal ophthalmia neonatorum.
expl: Corneal perforation is characteristic of gonococcal and Pseudomonas infection rather than staphylococcal conjunctivitis.

items.rationale: Amoxicillin remains first choice for uncomplicated acute otitis media because of its record of safety, relative efficacy, palatability, and low cost. It is the most efficacious available oral drug against both penicillin-susceptible and penicillin-nonsusceptible pneumococci.

High-dose amoxicillin for otitis media is given in 2 divided doses a day.

options: BMI of 30 kg/m² or more, regardless of age
BMI from the 85th to the 95th percentile for age and sex
BMI at or above the 95th percentile for age and sex
items.rationale: In children 2 years and older, obesity and overweight are defined by body mass index (BMI) percentiles: obesity is a BMI at or above the 95th percentile, and overweight is a BMI between the 85th and 95th percentiles.

Weight-for-age does not account for height and is not used to define obesity.
A BMI between the 85th and 95th percentiles defines overweight.

items.stem: Severe acute malnutrition includes severe wasting. Which weight-for-length (or height) z-score on the World Health Organization (WHO) Child Growth Standards defines severe wasting?
items.rationale: Severe acute malnutrition is defined as severe wasting, bilateral edema, or both. Severe wasting is a weight-for-length (or height) below −3 standard deviations (SD) of the WHO Child Growth Standards.

A z-score of zero is the median of the reference population.
A z-score below −2 SD defines wasting, but not severe wasting.

Fat is the most energy-dense macronutrient
Dietary cholesterol does not affect serum LDL
Atherosclerotic changes first appear in adolescence

expl: Trans fats behave like saturated fats and raise low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol.

Autopsy studies show that atherosclerosis begins early in childhood, even in infancy.

items.rationale: By third grade, children need to sustain attention through a 45-minute period as the curriculum grows more complex. Reading shifts from decoding words to understanding content, and from the third or fourth grade children increasingly enjoy strategy games and wordplay such as puns.
expl: A 60-minute period exceeds the 45 minutes expected by third grade.
A 15-minute span is well below what the third-grade curriculum requires.
A 30-minute span is below the 45-minute period expected by third grade.

items.stem: Jaundice is more common in premature than in term infants. Through which mechanism does prematurity usually cause or increase unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia?
options: Obstruction of bile flow from the liver
Inherited absence of the conjugating enzyme
Reduced activity of the hepatic conjugating enzyme
items.rationale: Jaundice occurs in about 80% of preterm infants, against about 60% of term infants. In neonates it usually results from the inability of an immature liver to conjugate bilirubin, which raises the indirect (unconjugated) fraction.
expl: Blood group incompatibility causes hemolysis at any gestational age; prematurity does not cause it.
Obstruction of bile flow raises conjugated (direct) bilirubin.
Inherited absence of the conjugating enzyme (Crigler-Najjar syndrome) is a genetic disorder that prematurity does not cause.

items.subject: Pediatrics
items.stem: A 7-year-old with fever and cough has dullness to percussion over the right lower chest. Which finding over that area indicates lobar consolidation rather than a pleural effusion?
options: Tracheal shift away from the dull side
Bronchial breath sounds with increased vocal resonance
Decreased breath sounds with reduced vocal resonance
Reduced chest movement on that side
items.rationale: Bronchial breath sounds heard over the periphery mean that the airways are open but the lung units are filled with liquid-like material, as in consolidation, and egophony confirms them. Vocal resonance is increased over lobar consolidation and decreased over a pleural effusion or empyema.
expl: A shift of the trachea away from the dull side suggests a large effusion pushing the mediastinum.
Decreased breath sounds with reduced vocal resonance point to a pleural effusion or empyema.
Reduced movement of the affected side occurs with both consolidation and effusion, so it does not separate them.

items.stem: A 9-year-old has newly diagnosed asthma with symptoms less than twice a month. The options use ICS for inhaled corticosteroid, SABA for short-acting beta-2 agonist, and LABA for long-acting beta-2 agonist. According to the Global Initiative for Asthma (GINA), what is the preferred first treatment?
options: Low-dose ICS taken whenever SABA is taken
As-needed SABA alone for symptom relief
items.rationale: GINA recommends ICS-containing treatment for all children 6 to 11 years old with asthma. At Step 1, for initial symptoms less than twice a month, taking ICS whenever SABA is taken for relief is preferred over regular ICS or as-needed SABA alone.

GINA prefers ICS taken with each SABA dose over as-needed SABA alone.
A daily leukotriene receptor antagonist is an alternative controller at a higher step, not the preferred first treatment.

items.stem: Under the definitions the World Health Organization (WHO) applied from 2021, extensively drug-resistant tuberculosis (XDR-TB) is multidrug-resistant TB (resistant to at least isoniazid and rifampicin) with additional resistance to which drugs?
options: Any fluoroquinolone plus amikacin, kanamycin, or capreomycin
Any fluoroquinolone plus bedaquiline or linezolid
items.rationale: Since January 2021, WHO defines XDR-TB as MDR/RR-TB that is also resistant to any fluoroquinolone and to at least one additional Group A drug; the Group A drugs are levofloxacin, moxifloxacin, bedaquiline, and linezolid. MDR/RR-TB with fluoroquinolone resistance alone is now pre-XDR-TB.
expl: Fluoroquinolone plus second-line injectable resistance was the definition used before 2021.
Pyrazinamide and ethambutol are first-line drugs, and resistance to them does not define XDR-TB.
Fluoroquinolone resistance on top of MDR/RR-TB now defines pre-XDR-TB.

items.rationale: An induration of 5 mm or more is positive in immunosuppressed people, including those on prolonged corticosteroids equivalent to 15 mg/day or more of prednisone or on TNF-alpha antagonists, as well as people with HIV and recent contacts of infectious TB.
expl: 20 mm is not a cutoff used to read the test.

15 mm is the cutoff for people with no known risk factors for TB.

items.subject: Pediatrics
items.stem: A 6-year-old boy has developmental delay, microcephaly, widely spaced eyes, and a small jaw. As an infant he had a high-pitched cry like a cat's. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.rationale: Cri-du-chat (5p minus) syndrome results from loss of part of chromosome 5. Infants often have a high-pitched, cat-like cry, and the disorder includes intellectual disability, microcephaly, hypotonia, widely set eyes, low-set ears, a small jaw, and a rounded face.
expl: Trisomy 21 causes hypotonia and characteristic facial features but not a cat-like cry.
Turner syndrome affects girls and causes short stature and ovarian failure, not a cat-like cry.
Prader-Willi syndrome causes neonatal hypotonia and later hyperphagia and obesity, not a cat-like cry.

items.subject: Pediatrics
items.stem: Over the past 4 weeks, a 4-year-old with asthma has had daytime wheezing about 3 times a week and has woken at night with cough twice. He has needed his reliever once a week and plays normally. Under the Global Initiative for Asthma (GINA), how is his symptom control classified?
items.rationale: For children 5 years and younger, GINA counts four features over the past 4 weeks: daytime symptoms more than once a week, any night waking or coughing from asthma, reliever use more than once a week, and any activity limitation. This child has 2 of the 4 (daytime symptoms and night waking), which is partly controlled; none is well controlled, and 3 or 4 is uncontrolled.
expl: Uncontrolled requires 3 or 4 of the features.
Symptom control is assessed over 4 weeks, and this history does not describe an acute exacerbation.
Well controlled requires none of the four features.

Night waking once and reliever use once a week
Reliever use every other day with normal sleep and play
Brief daytime cough once a week with normal play

Brief symptoms once a week with normal play meet no criterion, which is well controlled.

items.subject: Pediatrics
items.stem: Which statement about congenital central hypoventilation syndrome (CCHS) is correct?
options: It occurs mainly in preterm infants
It usually appears shortly after birth
Breathing rises normally when blood CO2 is high
items.rationale: People with CCHS hypoventilate, especially during sleep, because the autonomic response that normally drives deeper breathing when oxygen falls and carbon dioxide rises is impaired. Symptoms usually appear shortly after birth, when affected infants hypoventilate on falling asleep, and they need ventilatory support.
expl: CCHS is a genetic disorder of breathing control and is not a complication of prematurity.
Treatment is ventilatory support, by mechanical ventilation or a diaphragm pacemaker.
The breathing response to a rise in carbon dioxide is impaired in CCHS.

items.subject: Surgery
items.stem: Under the current (Sepsis-3) definitions, which finding defines septic shock?
options: Two or more SIRS criteria with a known infection
Organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated response to infection
Vasopressors needed to keep MAP ≥ 65 mm Hg despite fluids
Fever above 38 °C with a heart rate above 90/min
items.rationale: Sepsis is life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection. Septic shock is sepsis with persistent hypotension that requires vasopressors to keep the mean arterial pressure at 65 mm Hg or more, with a serum lactate above 2 mmol/L, despite adequate volume resuscitation. SIRS criteria are no longer part of the formal definition.
expl: SIRS criteria with an infection defined sepsis under older definitions and are not part of the current formal definition.
Organ dysfunction from a dysregulated response to infection defines sepsis, not septic shock.
Fever and tachycardia are SIRS criteria, not the definition of septic shock.

items.subject: Surgery
items.stem: After a motor vehicle crash, a 50-year-old man weighing 70 kg is anxious, with a heart rate of 110/min, a respiratory rate of 22/min, a normal systolic blood pressure, and a narrowed pulse pressure. What is his estimated blood loss?
items.rationale: These signs fit class 2 hemorrhage: a loss of 15 to 30% of blood volume (750 to 1500 mL in a 70-kg adult), with heart rate 100 to 120/min, respiratory rate 20 to 24/min, a narrowing pulse pressure, and a systolic pressure unchanged or slightly decreased. A significant fall in blood pressure, heart rate above 120/min, and declining urine output mark class 3.
expl: Class 1 loss (up to 750 mL) leaves the heart rate normal or minimally raised.
Class 3 loss (1500 to 2000 mL) brings a significant fall in blood pressure and heart rate above 120/min.
Class 4 loss (over 40%) causes hypotension, marked tachycardia, and minimal urine output.

options: Keep the patient warm to prevent hypothermia
Take a detailed history before the primary survey

Transport the patient to the nearest facility

items.stem: What is the classic triad of cardiac tamponade?
options: Jugular venous distension, third heart sound, hypotension
Jugular venous collapse, third heart sound, hypertension
Jugular venous collapse, muffled heart sounds, hypotension
Jugular venous distension, muffled heart sounds, hypotension
items.rationale: Beck's triad is hypotension, jugular venous distension, and muffled heart sounds. Distension reflects raised venous pressure from impaired right heart filling; pulsus paradoxus is also typical.
expl: A third heart sound is not part of the triad.
The neck veins are distended and the blood pressure is low.
The neck veins are distended, not collapsed.

items.stem: During the primary survey, a hypotensive patient with blunt abdominal trauma is evaluated for intra-abdominal bleeding. Which test is most appropriate?
items.rationale: Ultrasound (FAST) can be done during the initial assessment without moving the patient; it images the pericardium, both upper quadrants, and the pelvis for free fluid and is particularly useful in unstable patients. CT is preferred for stable patients, and diagnostic peritoneal lavage has largely been replaced by FAST and CT.
expl: CT is preferred for stable patients; unstable patients need immediate intervention rather than transfer to CT.
Diagnostic peritoneal lavage has largely been replaced by FAST and CT.
Laparoscopy is not a first test in an unstable patient.

Ask him to say his name

The Parkland formula estimates fluid needs, not burn size.

items.subject: Surgery
items.stem: In an asymptomatic patient with a pneumothorax managed without surgery, which gas in the pleural space diffuses into the capillaries fastest?
items.rationale: Carbon dioxide diffuses readily, much faster than oxygen, so it leaves the pleural space first. Nitrogen, the main component of the trapped air, diffuses slowly, which is why a pneumothorax resolves gradually (To verify). An asymptomatic primary spontaneous pneumothorax can be observed without treatment.
expl: Nitrogen diffuses slowly and makes up most of the trapped air.
Oxygen diffuses more slowly than carbon dioxide.
Freon is not a gas of the pleural space.

Extension beyond the wound margins defines a keloid.
Invasion of the surrounding skin defines a keloid.

items.subject: Surgery
items.stem: After tissue injury, what initiates coagulation in vivo?
options: Factor XII binding to subendothelial collagen
items.rationale: In vivo, coagulation starts when vessel injury brings blood into contact with tissue factor on perivascular cells; tissue factor binds factor VIIa, and the complex activates factor X (and factor IX), leading to thrombin and then fibrin. Contact activation by factor XII is not needed in vivo, and people lacking factor XII do not bleed.
expl: Factor XII contact activation is not required for coagulation in vivo.
Thrombin generation is a later step of the common pathway.
Fibrin formation is the final step of coagulation.

items.subject: Surgery
items.stem: What is the initial response to blood vessel injury?
items.rationale: Local vasoconstriction is an immediate reaction to injury and reduces blood loss. Platelet adhesion and aggregation then form a plug, coagulation generates fibrin, and fibrinolysis later removes the clot during repair of the vessel wall.
expl: Platelet plug formation follows vasoconstriction.
Fibrinolysis removes the clot during vessel repair.
Fibrin forms after the coagulation cascade is activated.

items.subject: Surgery
items.stem: A trauma patient is in hypovolemic shock from a closed femur fracture and a suspected splenic injury, with no external bleeding. What is the first priority?
items.rationale: The primary survey proceeds airway, breathing, circulation, disability, and exposure, so the airway is secured first. Circulation follows: external bleeding is controlled by direct pressure, IV access is placed, and fluids or blood are given; fractures are splinted pending full assessment.
expl: Hemorrhage control is part of circulation, which follows airway and breathing.
Fractures are splinted after life threats are addressed.
Volume restoration is part of circulation, after airway and breathing.

items.subject: Surgery
items.stem: What causes the respiratory distress and hypoxemia in tension pneumothorax?
items.rationale: Rising pleural pressure compresses the lung and impairs ventilation and oxygenation; blood still flowing through the collapsed, unventilated lung is a shunt, which lowers arterial oxygen. The pressure also shifts the mediastinum and impedes venous return, causing hypotension.
expl: ARDS is diffuse inflammatory lung injury, not the mechanism of tension pneumothorax.
Pump failure is not the cause; reduced venous return lowers cardiac output.
Pulmonary contusion is a separate lung injury.

items.subject: Surgery
items.stem: What causes the cardiovascular collapse in tension pneumothorax?
items.rationale: Pleural pressure rises until it shifts the mediastinum and compresses the heart, great vessels, and superior vena cava; impaired venous return lowers cardiac output and can cause hypotension and cardiac arrest within minutes. Treatment is immediate needle decompression without waiting for an x-ray.
expl: Shunting explains the hypoxemia, not the circulatory collapse.
Diaphragmatic movement does not explain the fall in cardiac output.
Wall motion abnormality reflects ischemia, not tension pneumothorax.

items.subject: Surgery
items.stem: After a motorcycle crash, a patient has BP 90/60 mmHg, heart rate 110/min, and respiratory rate 26/min, with air bubbling from a wound on the anterior neck. His airway has been secured. What is the next step?
options: Local wound exploration in the emergency department
Esophagram to look for esophageal perforation
Operative exploration and repair of the tracheal injury
items.rationale: Air bubbling from a neck wound suggests tracheal injury. The priorities are securing the airway, maintaining ventilation, controlling hemorrhage, and treating shock, and unstable patients with signs of vascular or aerodigestive injury go on to invasive intervention rather than further imaging or observation.
expl: Local exploration in the emergency department is not the treatment for an unstable patient with an airway injury.
Contrast studies are for stable patients, not an unstable patient with an obvious airway injury.
Observation is unsafe in an unstable patient with signs of aerodigestive injury.

items.subject: Surgery
items.stem: A 29-year-old man weighing 88 kg has partial- and full-thickness burns over 40% of his body surface. By the Parkland formula, at what rate (mL/hour) should fluid run during the first 8 hours after the burn?
items.rationale: Parkland: 4 mL × 88 kg × 40% = 14,080 mL in the first 24 hours after the burn. Half (7,040 mL) is given over the first 8 hours, which is 880 mL/hour, and the rest over the next 16 hours (440 mL/hour). The rate is then adjusted to urine output (0.5 mL/kg/hour in adults).
expl: 780 mL/hour falls short of the calculated rate.
1300 mL/hour exceeds the calculated rate.
550 mL/hour falls short of the calculated rate.

items.stem: A 28-year-old man has a dry, leathery burn on the right forearm that does not blanch and is painless to pinprick. What is its depth?
items.rationale: Full-thickness burns extend through the entire dermis; they may be white, charred, or brown and leathery, do not blanch, and are usually anesthetic. Superficial and superficial partial-thickness burns blanch and are painful, and deep partial-thickness burns do not blanch but still sense pinprick as pressure.
expl: Superficial partial-thickness burns blanch, are painful, and blister.
Superficial burns are red, blanch, and are painful.
Deep partial-thickness burns still perceive pinprick as pressure and are not leathery.

items.subject: Surgery
items.stem: Which structure must be identified and preserved during thyroidectomy to avoid vocal cord paralysis and hoarseness?
items.rationale: The recurrent laryngeal nerves supply the intrinsic laryngeal muscles (except the cricothyroid) and are identified and preserved during thyroidectomy; injury causes vocal cord paralysis and hoarseness. The parathyroid glands are also preserved to avoid hypoparathyroidism.
expl: The pyramidal lobe is thyroid tissue removed with the gland.
The ligament of Berry is divided to free the gland, although the nerve runs close to it.
The middle thyroid vein is the shortest thyroid vein and is divided during thyroidectomy.

items.stem: Which condition causes the greatest loss of body nitrogen?
items.rationale: Catabolic states such as burns, infection, and starvation break down body protein faster than it is replaced, producing a negative nitrogen balance. Energy needs rise with metabolic stress and are highest, up to about 45 kcal/kg/day, with severe trauma or burns.
expl: An uncomplicated elective operation causes modest, short-lived catabolism.
A self-limited viral illness causes only modest catabolism.
An isolated fracture causes less metabolic stress than extensive burns.

items.subject: Surgery
items.stem: In the classic trimodal distribution of trauma deaths, how are deaths in the first peak (at the scene, within minutes) best reduced?
items.rationale: Immediate deaths occur at the scene within minutes from nonsurvivable injuries, so they are reduced by injury prevention. Early deaths within hours are reduced by improved access to trauma care, and late deaths from organ failure and sepsis by better resuscitation and critical care.
expl: Operative care helps potentially survivable injuries, not immediately fatal ones.
Access to organized trauma care reduces early deaths within hours.
Critical care reduces late deaths from organ failure and sepsis.

items.subject: Surgery
items.stem: In which patient is acute limb ischemia most likely?
options: A 25-year-old with a crushed thigh and a cold, pulseless foot
A 35-year-old woman with episodic cold-induced color changes of the toes
A 40-year-old man with calf pain on walking for 2 years
A 60-year-old man with diabetes and long-standing dry gangrene of a toe
items.rationale: Acute limb ischemia is the sudden onset of pain, pallor, paresthesias, poikilothermia, and pulselessness (with paralysis in severe cases) from acute arterial occlusion by thrombus, embolus, dissection, or acute compartment syndrome; crush injuries are a common cause of compartment syndrome. Episodic color change suggests vasospasm, years of claudication are chronic peripheral artery disease, and long-standing dry gangrene is chronic ischemia.
expl: Episodic, cold-induced color change suggests vasospasm (Raynaud phenomenon), not arterial occlusion.
Exertional calf pain over years is claudication from chronic peripheral artery disease.
Long-standing dry gangrene reflects chronic, not acute, ischemia.

items.subject: Surgery
items.stem: A patient in the emergency department has a grossly displaced open tibial fracture with a wound larger than 1 cm (Gustilo-Anderson grade II). Which initial step is appropriate?
options: Cover the wound with a sterile dressing and give IV antibiotics
Push the exposed bone back under the skin
Close the wound primarily in the emergency department
items.rationale: Suspected open fractures need sterile wound dressings, tetanus prophylaxis, broad-spectrum IV antibiotics given early (for example, within 1 hour of arrival), splinting, and surgical irrigation and debridement to prevent infection. Grade II open fractures have a wound over 1 cm with moderate soft-tissue damage.
expl: IV antibiotics are given early, within about 1 hour of arrival.
Pushing contaminated bone back into the wound carries contamination into deep tissue.
Open fractures are irrigated and debrided surgically rather than closed in the emergency department.

items.subject: Surgery
items.topic: Perioperative care, fluids, and wound healing
items.stem: Which management decision differs between a heavily contaminated traumatic wound and a clean wound?
options: The need to ask about tetanus immunization
The timing and type of wound closure
The need for irrigation and debridement
items.rationale: All wounds are cleansed, explored, and debrided as needed, and tetanus status is checked. Uncontaminated wounds under about 6 to 8 hours old are usually closed primarily, whereas wounds with significant contamination are left open and closed after 3 to 5 days if no infection develops (delayed primary closure).
expl: Tetanus immunization status is checked for every traumatic wound.
Rabies prophylaxis depends on animal exposure, not on contamination.
Irrigation and debridement are done for both clean and contaminated wounds.

items.subject: Surgery
items.stem: In which type of shock is the main defect the inability of cells to use the oxygen delivered to them, despite a normal or high cardiac output?
items.rationale: In distributive shock such as sepsis, cardiac output and oxygen delivery may be high, but blood bypasses capillary beds through arteriovenous shunts and cellular oxygen transport is uncoupled, so oxygen consumption falls. Obstructive and hemorrhagic shock reduce oxygen delivery by lowering cardiac filling or blood volume.
expl: Shock after soft-tissue trauma is mainly hypovolemic, from lost blood and fluid.
Obstructive shock reduces cardiac filling and output.
Hemorrhagic shock reduces oxygen delivery by lowering blood volume.

items.subject: Surgery
items.stem: A man with a gunshot wound to the right chest has decreased breath sounds on the right, hypotension, tachycardia, tachypnea, and distended neck veins. What type of shock does he have?
items.rationale: Distended neck veins with hypotension and absent breath sounds after chest trauma point to tension pneumothorax, a cause of obstructive shock: raised intrathoracic pressure reduces venous return and cardiac filling. Hemorrhagic shock flattens the neck veins. Tension pneumothorax is decompressed immediately, followed by tube thoracostomy.
expl: Vasodilatory shock does not raise venous pressure.
Hemorrhagic shock causes flat, not distended, neck veins.
Septic shock does not follow minutes after a gunshot wound.

items.subject: Surgery
items.stem: A head-injured patient opens his eyes only to a painful stimulus, is confused but able to answer questions, and shows abnormal (decorticate) flexion to pain. What is his Glasgow Coma Scale score?
items.rationale: Eye opening to pain scores 2, confused speech that still answers questions scores 4, and abnormal (decorticate) flexion scores 3, for a total of 9. Withdrawal from pain would score 4 and eye opening to voice 3.
expl: 11 would need eye opening to voice and withdrawal from pain.
13 would need spontaneous eye opening and purposeful movement.
7 undercounts the verbal and motor scores.

items.subject: Surgery
items.stem: After a blow to the chest, a 21-year-old develops sudden right chest pain and dyspnea. He is hypotensive with distended neck veins, absent breath sounds and hyperresonance on the right, and a trachea deviated to the left. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.rationale: Absent breath sounds and hyperresonance on one side with tracheal deviation away from it, hypotension, and distended neck veins indicate tension pneumothorax, which is diagnosed clinically and decompressed immediately without waiting for an x-ray. Tamponade also causes hypotension and distended neck veins, but breath sounds are preserved.
expl: Tamponade does not cause unilateral absent breath sounds or tracheal deviation.
A rib fracture alone does not cause shock or tracheal deviation.
Pulmonary contusion causes hypoxemia without tracheal shift or obstructive shock.

items.subject: Surgery
items.stem: A 21-year-old man with a stab wound to the right chest has a chest tube placed. Thoracotomy is indicated if the initial chest tube drainage exceeds:
items.rationale: Urgent thoracotomy is indicated when initial bleeding exceeds 1500 mL, or when bleeding exceeds 200 mL/hour for 2 to 4 hours with respiratory or hemodynamic compromise or a need for repeated transfusion. Massive hemothorax is defined as rapid accumulation of 1500 mL or more.
expl: 1000 mL of initial drainage is below the threshold.
The threshold is 1500 mL; waiting for 2000 mL delays needed surgery.
500 mL of initial drainage does not by itself indicate thoracotomy.

items.subject: Surgery
items.stem: During IV fluid resuscitation of an adult with burns over 20% of body surface area, what urine output is targeted?
items.rationale: Adults with burns over 20% TBSA (10% to 15% in children) need formal fluid resuscitation. The rate from the Parkland formula is adjusted to a urine output of about 0.5 to 1.0 mL/kg/hour (30 to 50 mL/hour) in adults, along with a systolic pressure above 90 mm Hg and normal mentation; children under 30 kg are kept at 1 mL/kg/hour.
expl: 4 to 5 mL/kg/hour signals excessive fluid administration.
2 to 3 mL/kg/hour exceeds the target and risks fluid overload.
0.1 to 0.2 mL/kg/hour indicates under-resuscitation.

items.stem: Which change characterizes the maturation (remodeling) phase of wound healing?
options: Tensile strength returns to 100% within a year
Type III collagen is replaced by type I collagen
items.rationale: Remodeling begins around day 21 and can continue for a year. Type III collagen is replaced by stronger type I collagen, which gradually increases tensile strength, but the scar reaches only about 80% of the strength of the original tissue. Fibroblasts undergo apoptosis, leaving a relatively acellular scar.
expl: Scar strength reaches only about 80% of the original tissue.
Fibroblast apoptosis leaves the mature wound relatively acellular.
Granulation tissue formation ends and the wound becomes less vascular (To verify).

items.subject: Surgery
items.stem: Which thresholds define the respiratory criterion of the systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS)?
options: Respiratory rate > 20/min or PaCO2 < 32 mm Hg
Respiratory rate > 16/min or PaCO2 < 40 mm Hg
Respiratory rate > 30/min or PaCO2 < 25 mm Hg
Respiratory rate > 10/min or PaCO2 < 22 mm Hg
items.rationale: SIRS is present when 2 or more of the following are met: temperature above 38 °C or below 36 °C, heart rate above 90/min, respiratory rate above 20/min or PaCO2 below 32 mm Hg, and WBC count above 12,000/µL, below 4,000/µL, or more than 10% band forms. SIRS criteria are no longer part of the formal definition of sepsis but are still used to flag possible sepsis.
expl: A rate above 16/min and a PaCO2 below 40 mm Hg are looser than the SIRS thresholds.
A rate above 30/min meets the criterion, but the defining thresholds are 20/min and 32 mm Hg.
The SIRS thresholds are a rate above 20/min and a PaCO2 below 32 mm Hg.

items.subject: Surgery
items.stem: Which test screens the intrinsic and common coagulation pathways and is used to monitor unfractionated heparin therapy?
items.rationale: The aPTT screens the factors of the intrinsic and common pathways (all factors except VII and XIII). Heparin prolongs the aPTT, so it is often used to monitor heparin therapy. The PT screens the extrinsic and common pathways and is reported as the INR.
expl: Whole-blood clotting time is an older, poorly standardized test that the aPTT has replaced (To verify).
The bleeding time is not reproducible enough to be reliable for clinical decisions.
The PT screens the extrinsic and common pathways (factors VII, X, V, II, and fibrinogen).

items.stem: When antiplatelet therapy must be interrupted for an elective operation, how long before surgery are agents such as aspirin and clopidogrel usually stopped?
items.rationale: Aspirin binds irreversibly to platelets, and platelets circulate for 7 to 10 days. In most cases, antiplatelet agents are stopped 5 to 7 days before surgery. Direct oral anticoagulants are timed instead by their half-life and the patient's renal function.
expl: 48 to 72 hours is shorter than the usual 5 to 7 days.
24 to 48 hours is shorter than the usual 5 to 7 days.
12 to 24 hours is far shorter than the usual 5 to 7 days.

items.subject: Surgery
items.stem: Which events make up primary hemostasis after a blood vessel is injured?
options: Vasodilation of the vessel with platelet inhibition
Activation of the coagulation cascade to form fibrin
Vasoconstriction and formation of a platelet plug
Fibrinolysis of the formed clot by plasmin
items.rationale: Hemostasis proceeds in 4 stages: constriction of the injured vessel, formation of a temporary platelet plug, activation of the coagulation cascade, and formation of the fibrin plug. Vasoconstriction is the immediate reaction to injury; platelets then adhere to the damaged intima and aggregate into the primary platelet plug.
expl: Prostacyclin and nitric oxide dilate intact vessels and prevent platelet aggregation; their production stops when the endothelium is disrupted.
Coagulation cascade activation and fibrin formation are the third and fourth stages, after the platelet plug.
Fibrinolysis by plasmin dissolves a clot after hemostasis and does not form one (To verify).

items.subject: Surgery
items.stem: In the Surviving Sepsis Campaign bundle, a crystalloid fluid challenge (at least 30 mL/kg) is given to a patient with sepsis who has hypotension or a serum lactate of at least what level?
items.rationale: The bundle comprises lactate measurement, blood cultures drawn before antibiotics, prompt broad-spectrum antibiotics, and a fluid challenge for a mean arterial pressure below 65 mm Hg or a lactate of 4 mmol/L or greater. The 2021 guideline suggests at least 30 mL/kg of IV crystalloid within the first 3 hours for sepsis-induced hypoperfusion or septic shock.
expl: Waiting for a lactate of 8 mmol/L would delay fluid that is indicated at 4 mmol/L.
A lactate above 2 mmol/L with vasopressor-dependent hypotension defines septic shock; the bundle's fluid trigger is 4 mmol/L.
A lactate of 1 mmol/L is below even the 2 mmol/L level used in the septic shock definition.

items.stem: About how many kilocalories per kilogram per day does a healthy adult need to maintain basal metabolism?
items.rationale: An adult's basal metabolic rate is about 1 kcal/kg per hour, which is about 24 kcal/kg per day (1,500 to 1,800 kcal/day). Total energy expenditure adds activity and metabolic stress; it ranges from as low as 20 kcal/kg/day to as high as 45 kcal/kg/day in severe metabolic stress such as trauma or burns.
expl: 30 to 35 kcal/kg/day exceeds basal needs and reflects added activity or stress (To verify).
10 to 15 kcal/kg/day is below the basal rate of about 24 kcal/kg/day.
40 to 45 kcal/kg/day approaches the requirement in severe metabolic stress.

items.subject: Surgery
items.stem: A patient with septic shock is hypotensive on arrival. What is the first-line intervention to restore perfusion?
options: IV infusion of a balanced isotonic crystalloid
Vasopressor infusion before any IV fluid
items.rationale: IV fluid is the first-line intervention in septic shock, and balanced isotonic crystalloid is preferred: 1 L is infused rapidly, and most patients need at least 30 mL/kg in the first 3 hours. Vasopressors such as norepinephrine are added when profound hypotension persists after initial fluid replacement.
expl: Blood products take priority in hemorrhagic shock; this patient's shock is septic.
Starch-based fluids such as hydroxyethyl starch increase mortality and should not be used.
Vasopressors are added for profound hypotension after initial fluid replacement.

items.stem: What is the most common cause of cardiogenic shock?
items.rationale: Acute myocardial infarction is the most common cause: ischemic or infarcted myocardium cannot contract normally, so stroke volume and cardiac output fall. About 5% to 10% of patients with acute MI develop cardiogenic shock. Disorders of the myocardium, valves, conduction system, or pericardium can also cause it.
expl: Cardiomyopathy is a less common cause than acute MI.
Myocarditis is a less common cause than acute MI.
Conduction system disorders can cause cardiogenic shock, but less often than acute MI.

items.subject: Surgery
items.stem: Which topical burn agent can cause hyponatremia when applied to large burned areas over a long period?
items.rationale: Silver nitrate 0.5% solution is kept continuously wet on the dressings. As the silver precipitates, the remaining free water in contact with the wound can cause hyponatremia and hypochloremia when it is applied to large surface areas, so electrolytes are monitored.
expl: Mafenide acetate is a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor and may cause metabolic acidemia.
Nitrofurazone is not associated with hyponatremia (To verify).
Silver sulfadiazine may cause transient leukopenia.

items.subject: Surgery
items.stem: Which acyanotic heart defect, caused by maldevelopment of the endocardial cushions, is characteristically associated with Down syndrome?
items.rationale: An atrioventricular septal defect (an ostium primum atrial septal defect with a common AV valve, with or without an inlet VSD) results from maldevelopment of the endocardial cushions and causes a left-to-right shunt. The majority of patients with the complete form have Down syndrome. About 50% of neonates with Down syndrome have congenital heart disease, most often VSD or AV septal defect.
expl: VSD is also common in Down syndrome, but an isolated VSD is not an endocardial cushion defect (To verify).
An ostium secundum defect lies in the fossa ovalis in the center of the atrial septum.
PDA is persistence of the fetal ductus arteriosus between the aorta and pulmonary artery.

items.stem: Which statement about cleft lip is correct?
options: It is commonly accompanied by a cleft palate
It usually involves the palate behind the incisive foramen
It occurs in about 1 in 10 live births
It results from failure of the palatal shelves to fuse
items.rationale: Cleft lip results from failure of the medial nasal process to fuse with the maxillary process and usually involves the primary palate anterior to the incisive foramen. Because the lip and primary palate form at the same stage of development, cleft lip is commonly associated with a cleft palate. The overall risk of cleft lip with or without cleft palate is about 0.1%.

The risk is about 0.1% (1 in 1,000), not 1 in 10.

Anisocoria is a difference in pupil size.
Glaucoma is progressive optic nerve damage related to a relative increase in intraocular pressure.

items.stem: A 32-year-old woman has a red eye with minimal pain, no discharge, and no photophobia. Visual acuity is 20/20, and the pupils are normal. The redness is confined to one sector of the globe and blanches with phenylephrine eye drops. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.rationale: Episcleritis causes a localized area of hyperemia with mild irritation, much less lacrimation than conjunctivitis, and no discharge. It is distinguished from scleritis by the lack of photophobia and severe pain. Phenylephrine 2.5% blanches a red eye unless the cause is scleritis.

Conjunctivitis reddens the whole bulbar and palpebral conjunctiva and causes more lacrimation and discharge.
Scleritis causes severe pain, and its redness does not blanch with phenylephrine.

items.stem: A child has a flat (type B) tympanogram with a normal ear-canal volume. What does this finding indicate?
options: Fixation of the stapes in otosclerosis
items.rationale: Tympanometry measures the impedance of the middle ear as ear-canal pressure is varied and is commonly used to screen children for middle ear effusion. A flat type B tracing with a normal ear-canal volume supports middle ear effusion; a flat tracing with a large volume suggests a perforation or a patent tympanostomy tube.
expl: Ossicular chain disruption makes the middle ear excessively compliant.
A normal middle ear shows maximal compliance when ear-canal pressure equals atmospheric pressure.
Stapes fixation in otosclerosis gives normal or reduced compliance.

items.stem: Which ECG change appears first as serum potassium rises above 5.5 mEq/L?
items.rationale: Hyperkalemia changes the ECG in a dose-dependent order: tall, peaked T waves at about 5.5 to 6.5 mEq/L; flattening or loss of P waves at 6.5 to 7.5 mEq/L; QRS widening at 7 to 8 mEq/L; and arrhythmias, a sine-wave pattern, and asystole at higher levels. Hyperkalemia also lengthens the PR interval and shortens the QT interval.
expl: Hypocalcemia prolongs the QT interval; hyperkalemia shortens it.
ST-segment sagging and T-wave depression are signs of hypokalemia.
Prominent U waves are a sign of hypokalemia.

items.rationale: One platelet concentrate unit increases the platelet count by approximately 10,000/µL. A count of about 10,000/µL is adequate for hemostasis in a patient without complicating conditions, and about 50,000/µL is needed for major surgery.

items.subject: Surgery
items.stem: Which is an example of distributive shock?
options: Tissue hypoxia from carbon monoxide poisoning
Hemorrhagic shock after a liver laceration
Neurogenic shock after a high spinal cord injury
items.rationale: Distributive shock results from arterial or venous vasodilation that makes a normal blood volume relatively inadequate. Causes include sepsis, anaphylaxis, and severe spinal cord injury, usually above T4 (neurogenic shock).
expl: Carbon monoxide binds hemoglobin with high affinity and prevents oxygen transport; it is not a class of shock (To verify).
Hemorrhagic shock is hypovolemic shock caused by bleeding.
Cardiogenic shock is a reduction in cardiac output due to a primary cardiac disorder.

items.subject: Surgery
items.stem: Six hours after an extensive anterior myocardial infarction, a 64-year-old man becomes hypotensive with cool, clammy skin, confusion, and oliguria. What type of shock is this most likely to be?
items.rationale: Cardiogenic shock is a reduction in cardiac output due to a primary cardiac disorder. In myocardial infarction, ischemic or infarcted myocardium cannot contract normally, so stroke volume and cardiac output fall; about 5% to 10% of patients with acute MI develop cardiogenic shock. Cool, clammy skin, confusion, and oliguria are signs of hypoperfusion seen in any type of shock.
expl: Neurogenic shock follows severe spinal cord injury, usually above T4.
Obstructive shock results from mechanical interference with filling or emptying of the heart, such as tension pneumothorax or tamponade.
Hypovolemic shock results from a critical decrease in intravascular volume, such as bleeding.

items.topic: Perioperative care, fluids, and wound healing
items.stem: A patient has a serum potassium of 6.3 mEq/L, and the ECG shows peaked T waves and flattened P waves. Which treatment should be given first?
items.rationale: When hyperkalemia causes ECG changes, IV calcium is given first because it stabilizes cardiac membranes, although it does not lower serum potassium. Insulin with glucose and, as an adjunct, a high-dose inhaled beta-2 agonist then shift potassium into cells, and potassium is removed from the body with resins or hemodialysis.
expl: Inhaled albuterol is an adjunct that lowers potassium by 0.5 to 1.5 mEq/L, with a peak effect at 90 minutes.
Insulin with glucose shifts potassium into cells; it is given with or after calcium when the ECG is abnormal.
Sodium polystyrene sulfonate acts slowly and often fails to lower potassium significantly.

items.subject: Surgery
items.stem: Which cytokine is anti-inflammatory?
items.rationale: Anti-inflammatory cytokines are immunoregulatory molecules that control the pro-inflammatory cytokine response; the major ones include IL-1 receptor antagonist, IL-4, IL-10, IL-11, and IL-13. Pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α are produced mainly by activated macrophages and up-regulate inflammatory reactions.
expl: IL-1 is a pro-inflammatory cytokine.
TNF-α is a pro-inflammatory cytokine.
IL-3 promotes the growth of hematopoietic progenitor cells.

items.stem: About how many kilocalories per kilogram per day does an adult need during severe metabolic stress, such as major trauma or burns?
items.rationale: Total energy expenditure varies with weight, activity, and metabolic stress; in adults it ranges from as low as 20 kcal/kg/day to as high as 45 kcal/kg/day in severe metabolic stress such as trauma or burns. Basal needs are about 1 kcal/kg per hour, or about 24 kcal/kg/day.
expl: 25 to 30 kcal/kg/day is below the requirement in severe stress (To verify).
55 to 60 kcal/kg/day exceeds the upper estimate of about 45 kcal/kg/day.
20 to 25 kcal/kg/day covers only basal metabolism.

items.subject: Surgery
items.stem: What is the most common microbiology of a necrotizing soft-tissue infection?
items.rationale: Necrotizing soft-tissue infection is a severe, rapidly spreading infection that causes extensive necrosis of the subcutaneous tissues and fascia. It is often polymicrobial (aerobic and/or anaerobic) but sometimes monomicrobial, for example streptococcal. Polymicrobial (type 1) necrotizing fasciitis is likely when the source is the bowel.
expl: A single gram-negative organism is not the usual pattern; most infections are mixed.
Monomicrobial infection, for example streptococcal, occurs sometimes but is less common.
Anaerobes usually occur with aerobes in a mixed infection.

items.stem: A patient has a tender, fluctuant nodule around a hair follicle that keeps enlarging despite warm compresses. What is the best management?
items.rationale: A tender nodule involving a hair follicle is a furuncle, a type of skin abscess usually caused by staphylococci. Warm compresses can speed drainage of a small abscess, but an enlarging, painful abscess is treated by incision and drainage, sometimes with antibiotics.
expl: Topical antibiotics do not treat an abscess; it must be drained.
Oral antibiotics are only sometimes added to incision and drainage.
IV antibiotics do not replace drainage of an abscess.

items.stem: Which epidermal layer is present only in the thick skin of the palms and soles?
items.rationale: From deepest to most superficial, the epidermal layers are the stratum basale, spinosum, granulosum, lucidum, and corneum. The stratum lucidum, 2 to 3 cell layers thick, is present only in the hairless thick skin of the palms and soles.
expl: The stratum corneum is the uppermost layer of all epidermis.
The stratum spinosum (prickle cell layer) is a layer of all epidermis.
The stratum basale, where cell division occurs, is a layer of all epidermis.

items.subject: Surgery
items.stem: Which hormone increases in response to tumor necrosis factor (TNF) as part of the stress response to infection or injury?
items.rationale: TNF is a mediator of the metabolic and stress hormone response to infection. TNF infusion in dogs increased plasma catecholamines, cortisol, and glucagon in a dose-dependent manner, and intravenous TNF in healthy men caused a transient stress hormone response along with a transient fall in serum testosterone.
expl: Estrogen is not part of the TNF-induced stress hormone response (To verify).
Serum testosterone falls transiently after TNF.
Human chorionic gonadotropin is a placental hormone and is not part of this response (To verify).

items.subject: Surgery
items.stem: An abdominal x-ray shows pneumoperitoneum, but the site of the bowel perforation is not identified. What is the next step in management?
items.rationale: Free air on imaging establishes the diagnosis of gastrointestinal perforation. Once a perforation is noted, immediate surgery is necessary because mortality from peritonitis rises rapidly the longer treatment is delayed; surgical repair is combined with IV fluid resuscitation and antibiotics. The site is found at operation.
expl: An erect chest x-ray would only confirm free air that has already been seen.
A supine radiograph adds nothing once free air is shown and delays surgery.
Peritoneal lavage is unnecessary once free air confirms a perforation (To verify).

items.topic: Perioperative care, fluids, and wound healing
items.stem: Which complication after bowel resection is promoted by preoperative malnutrition and carries the greatest morbidity and mortality?
items.rationale: Weight loss and malnutrition before surgery have an important role in anastomotic dehiscence, and an anastomotic leak after colorectal surgery is a major complication that increases postoperative morbidity and mortality. Malnutrition impairs wound healing in proportion to the loss of lean body mass.
expl: Ileus delays recovery but carries less morbidity than an anastomotic leak (To verify).
Atelectasis is common after anesthesia and usually resolves with lung expansion (To verify).
Phlebitis is related to the IV catheter and is a minor complication (To verify).

items.subject: Surgery
items.stem: A 20-year-old woman has persistent hypogastric pain, hypotension, tachycardia, and cold, clammy extremities. Her pregnancy test is positive. What type of shock does she most likely have?
items.rationale: Shock with a positive pregnancy test suggests a ruptured ectopic pregnancy, which causes occult bleeding and hemorrhagic (hypovolemic) shock from a critical decrease in intravascular volume.
expl: Neurogenic shock follows severe spinal cord injury, usually above T4.
Septic shock arises from infection and is typically accompanied by fever.
Cardiogenic shock follows a primary cardiac disorder such as myocardial infarction.

items.subject: Surgery
items.stem: After a colon resection, a 25-year-old man develops a surgical site infection that delays his discharge. How is this event classified?
items.rationale: An adverse event is any injury caused by medical care, such as a postoperative wound infection; the Harvard Medical Practice Study definition includes injury that prolongs hospitalization. The label does not imply error or negligence: a wound infection counts as an adverse event even when sterile technique and antibiotic prophylaxis were optimal.
expl: Negligence requires care that fell below the expected standard, which is not stated here.
A sentinel event involves death or serious harm, such as surgery on the wrong patient or body part.
A near miss is an event that did not injure the patient, only because of chance.

items.subject: Surgery
items.stem: On dermoscopy, which finding points to a melanocytic lesion rather than basal cell carcinoma?
items.rationale: The hallmark dermoscopic feature of basal cell carcinoma is well-focused arborizing (tree-like branching) vessels; other findings include multiple blue-gray globules, leaf-like structures, large blue-gray ovoid nests, and spoke-wheel areas. Basal cell carcinoma lacks the pigment network seen in melanocytic lesions.
expl: Large blue-gray ovoid nests are a feature of basal cell carcinoma.
Arborizing vessels are the hallmark of basal cell carcinoma.
Multiple blue-gray globules are a feature of basal cell carcinoma.

items.subject: Surgery
items.stem: Which artery supplying the stomach arises directly from the celiac trunk?
items.rationale: The celiac trunk gives rise to the common hepatic, splenic, and left gastric arteries. The right gastric artery arises from the proper hepatic artery, the left gastroepiploic artery from the splenic artery, and the right gastroepiploic artery from the gastroduodenal artery. The left gastric artery supplies the lesser curvature and distal esophagus and anastomoses with the right gastric artery.
expl: The left gastroepiploic artery arises from the splenic artery.
The right gastric artery arises from the proper hepatic artery.
The right gastroepiploic artery arises from the gastroduodenal artery.

items.subject: Surgery
items.stem: Where laparoscopic equipment and expertise are available, what is the preferred treatment for uncomplicated acute appendicitis?
options: Antibiotics covering gram-positive organisms and anaerobes
items.rationale: The WSES 2020 guidelines recommend laparoscopic appendectomy as the preferred approach over open appendectomy for uncomplicated and complicated appendicitis where equipment and expertise are available. An antibiotic-first strategy can be considered in selected patients with uncomplicated appendicitis, but it fails during the first admission in about 8% and leads to readmission for recurrence within 1 year in about 20%.
expl: Antibiotic treatment is an option only in selected patients and must cover enteric gram-negative organisms and anaerobes.
Observation alone is not the preferred treatment (To verify).
Open appendectomy is the alternative when laparoscopy is not available.

items.subject: Surgery
items.stem: Mechanical small bowel obstruction is classified by the location of the obstructing lesion. Which is an intramural cause?
items.rationale: Intraluminal causes lie within the lumen (for example, gallstone ileus), intramural causes arise in the bowel wall (for example, tumors), and extrinsic causes act from outside (for example, adhesions). In Crohn disease, transmural inflammation thickens the bowel wall, and fibrosis and stricture formation can obstruct it.
expl: A trichobezoar is a hair mass within the lumen, an intraluminal cause (To verify).
A hernia obstructs the bowel from outside its wall (To verify).
Adhesions are an extrinsic cause and the most common cause of small bowel obstruction.

items.subject: Surgery
items.stem: A 74-year-old man with known diverticulosis undergoes emergency laparotomy for 2 days of severe abdominal pain. Purulent fluid is found in all 4 quadrants, with a perforated sigmoid diverticulum and no fecal contamination. What is his Hinchey stage?
items.rationale: The Hinchey classification has 4 stages of perforated diverticulitis: I, pericolic abscess or phlegmon; II, pelvic, intra-abdominal, or retroperitoneal abscess (modified as IIa, a distant abscess amenable to percutaneous drainage, and IIb, a complex abscess with fistula); III, generalized purulent peritonitis; and IV, generalized fecal peritonitis.
expl: Hinchey IIb is a complex abscess associated with a fistula.
Hinchey IV is generalized fecal peritonitis.
Hinchey IIa is a distant abscess amenable to percutaneous drainage.

items.subject: Surgery
items.stem: A patient has a strangulated inguinal hernia. What is the next step in management?
options: Manual reduction in the emergency room
CT scan to confirm the diagnosis
items.rationale: An incarcerated or strangulated hernia of any kind requires urgent surgical repair. Gangrene and perforation of the gut can occur within 6 hours when the intestinal blood supply is interrupted, and advanced imaging must not delay surgery when the symptoms and signs are definitive.
expl: Elective repair is for hernias that are not incarcerated or strangulated (To verify).
Manual reduction of a strangulated hernia risks returning nonviable bowel to the abdomen (To verify).
Advanced imaging must not delay surgery when the symptoms and signs are definitive.

items.subject: Surgery
items.stem: Which description fits imperforate anus (anal atresia)?
options: No anal opening; the anal canal is closed by a membrane or thicker tissue
Absent ganglion cells in the distal bowel from failed neural crest migration
Narrowing of the pyloric channel from hypertrophied muscle
A normally placed anus without functioning sphincter muscles
items.rationale: In anal atresia, the tissue closing the anus may be a thin membrane of skin or several centimeters thick, from failure of the anal pit to develop or from atresia of the rectum. In high lesions, a fistula often runs to the perineum or urethra in males and to the vagina in females, and half or more of affected infants have other anomalies.
expl: Absent ganglion cells from failed neural crest migration define Hirschsprung disease.
Hypertrophy of the pyloric muscle causes hypertrophic pyloric stenosis.
A normally placed anus without sphincter function is not anal atresia (To verify).

items.subject: Surgery
items.stem: What is the most common primary malignant intraocular tumor of childhood?
items.rationale: Retinoblastoma is the most common primary intraocular cancer of childhood, accounting for about 3% of pediatric malignancies, and is most often diagnosed before age 2. Choroidal (uveal) melanoma is the most common cancer originating in the eye overall and occurs most often at age 55 to 60.
expl: Rhabdomyosarcoma is a malignant tumor of the orbit, outside the eye itself.
Ocular toxocariasis is a parasitic infection, not a tumor (To verify).
Choroidal melanoma is the most common primary eye cancer overall, mainly in adults aged 55 to 60.

items.stem: What is the normal pathway of tear drainage?
options: Lacrimal sac, punctum, canaliculi, nasolacrimal duct
Punctum, lacrimal sac, canaliculi, nasolacrimal duct
Lacrimal sac, canaliculi, punctum, nasolacrimal duct
Punctum, canaliculi, lacrimal sac, nasolacrimal duct

expl: The punctum is the entry point of the system, before the lacrimal sac.
The canaliculi lie between the punctum and the lacrimal sac.
Tears enter at the punctum and pass through the canaliculi before reaching the lacrimal sac.

items.stem: What is the expected outcome when a patient loses 40% or more of lean body mass?
options: Pressure sores and failure of wound healing
items.rationale: Complications track the proportion of lean body mass lost: about 10% impairs immunity and increases infection; 20% decreases healing and causes weakness; 30% leaves the patient too weak to sit, with pressure sores, pneumonia, and no healing; and 40% causes death, usually from pneumonia.
expl: Decreased healing and weakness occur at about 20% loss.
Impaired immunity and increased infection occur at about 10% loss.
Pressure sores and failure to heal occur at about 30% loss.

items.stem: Which feature makes spontaneous closure of an enterocutaneous fistula more likely?
items.rationale: Low-output fistulas drain less than 200 mL/day and high-output fistulas more than 500 mL/day. Short, wide, high-output fistulas tend to stay open, whereas long, narrow, low-output fistulas are more likely to close. Factors that keep a fistula open are remembered as FRIEND: foreign body, radiation, inflammation or infection, epithelialization of the tract, neoplasm, and distal obstruction.
expl: Epithelialization of the tract keeps the fistula open.
Radiation is one of the factors that keep a fistula open.
A short tract favors persistence; long, narrow tracts are more likely to close.

options: Local (wedge) resection without lymph node dissection
Proximal gastrectomy with lymph node dissection

items.subject: Surgery
items.stem: What is the main clinical use of Goodsall's rule in anal fistula?
options: Detecting an abscess along the fistula tract
Determining how much sphincter the tract involves
Predicting the location of the internal opening
items.rationale: Goodsall's rule predicts the location of the internal opening from the external opening, with up to 75% accuracy. Anterior fistulas with an external opening within 3 cm of the anal verge run radially to an internal opening at the same clock position; posterior fistulas and those opening farther than 3 cm away curve to an internal opening in the posterior midline at 6 o'clock.
expl: Abscesses are identified with endoanal ultrasound or MRI.
The tract's relation to the sphincter is defined with endoanal ultrasound or MRI.
Goodsall's rule does not estimate recurrence (To verify).

items.stem: Which statement about the treatment of acute appendicitis is correct?
options: Nonoperative treatment fails in more than 50% of patients in the short term
Appendectomy remains the standard treatment for uncomplicated appendicitis
Appendicitis recurs in more than 90% of patients after nonoperative treatment
Every patient in whom nonoperative treatment fails has complicated appendicitis
items.rationale: Antibiotics alone resolve most uncomplicated appendicitis during the first admission, but a significant number of patients have a recurrence and need appendectomy within the following year, so appendectomy is still recommended. Antibiotic treatment fails during the first admission in about 8%, about 20% more are readmitted for recurrence within 1 year, and late recurrence reached 39% at 5 years in the APPAC trial.
expl: Failure during the first admission is about 8%, with about 20% more readmitted within 1 year.
Recurrence after 5 years was about 39% in the APPAC trial.
Only 2.3% of patients operated on for recurrence had complicated appendicitis.

items.stem: How is the psoas sign elicited in a patient with suspected appendicitis?
options: Guarding with rebound tenderness in the right lower quadrant
Pain in the right lower quadrant on palpation of the left lower quadrant
Pain on passive internal rotation of the flexed right thigh
Pain on passive extension of the right hip, which stretches the iliopsoas
items.rationale: The psoas sign is increased pain on passive extension of the right hip, which stretches the iliopsoas muscle over an inflamed retrocecal appendix. Pain in the right lower quadrant on palpation of the left lower quadrant is Rovsing sign, and pain on passive internal rotation of the flexed thigh is the obturator sign.
expl: Guarding and rebound tenderness are signs of peritoneal irritation, not the psoas sign (To verify).

items.subject: Surgery
items.stem: After a laparoscopic transabdominal preperitoneal (TAPP) repair of a right inguinal hernia, a 40-year-old man has decreased sensation over the anterior and lateral right thigh. Which nerve is most likely injured?
options: Genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve
Femoral branch of the genitofemoral nerve
items.rationale: The lateral femoral cutaneous nerve is a purely sensory nerve of the anterolateral thigh. In laparoscopic repair it lies with the femoral branch of the genitofemoral nerve in the triangle of pain, and it is the nerve most commonly injured, followed by the genitofemoral nerve; laparoscopic inguinal repair is a recognized cause of meralgia paresthetica.
expl: The genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve runs in the spermatic cord to the genital region (To verify).
The femoral branch of the genitofemoral nerve supplies a small area of the upper anterior thigh rather than the lateral thigh (To verify).
The iliohypogastric nerve is protected by keeping lateral dissection superficial to the transversalis fascia and does not supply the lateral thigh (To verify).

items.subject: Surgery
items.stem: What is the body's first line of defense against infection?
items.rationale: The skin, corneas, and mucosa of the respiratory, gastrointestinal, and genitourinary tracts form a physical barrier that is the body's first line of defense. When the barrier is breached, innate immunity (including complement and phagocytes) responds immediately, and acquired immunity, including antibodies, develops after exposure to an antigen.
expl: Macrophages and other phagocytes act after the physical barrier has been breached.
Complement acts after the physical barrier has been breached.
Antibodies are part of acquired immunity, which develops after exposure to an antigen.

items.stem: In a critically ill patient receiving fluid resuscitation, which bedside measure is the most useful guide to hydration and perfusion?
options: Heart rate and blood pressure alone
A single central venous pressure reading
Skin turgor and capillary refill time
items.rationale: Urine output, measured hourly through a urinary catheter, is a good indicator of renal perfusion; during resuscitation, the blood pressure response, lactate clearance, and most importantly urine output (target at least 0.5 mL/kg/hour) guide fluid therapy. A single central venous pressure value can mislead, because it may be raised in hypovolemic patients with pulmonary hypertension.
expl: Heart rate and blood pressure can stay near normal despite hypoperfusion (To verify).
CVP may be raised in hypovolemic patients with preexisting pulmonary hypertension, so a single reading can mislead.
Skin turgor and capillary refill are imprecise guides in critically ill adults (To verify).

items.rationale: Liposarcoma is the most common soft-tissue sarcoma in adults, about 20% of cases, arising most often in the extremities and retroperitoneum. Undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma (formerly malignant fibrous histiocytoma) is one of the most common high-grade subtypes, at about 5% to 10%.

Synovial sarcoma is less common than liposarcoma (To verify).

items.stem: Which woman has the highest risk of invasive ductal carcinoma of the breast?
options: A 58-year-old with menarche at 15 who has never been pregnant
A 60-year-old with menarche at 12 and 3 term pregnancies
A 45-year-old with menarche at 16 and 2 term pregnancies
A 61-year-old with menarche at 11 who has never been pregnant
items.rationale: Breast cancer risk rises with age, and reproductive risk factors include menarche before age 12, first live birth after age 30, nulliparity, and menopause after age 55. The 61-year-old with menarche at 11 who has never been pregnant combines older age, early menarche, and nulliparity.
expl: Menarche at 15 is not early, so this woman lacks one of the risk factors.
Menarche at 12 is not before age 12, and she has had 3 term pregnancies.
This younger woman with late menarche and 2 term pregnancies has the fewest risk factors.

items.stem: Which type of skin graft gives the least secondary contraction, the best cosmetic result, and the greatest durability?
items.rationale: Full-thickness skin grafts include the entire epidermis and dermis, giving better cosmesis, less contraction, greater durability, and greater resistance to trauma than split-thickness grafts, which lack the deeper dermis and skin appendages. They need a well-vascularized recipient bed and suit small defects of the face, hands, and ears.
expl: A meshed split-thickness graft covers a larger area but contracts and heals with a meshed pattern (To verify).
A composite graft contains skin with other tissue such as cartilage and is used for small specialized defects (To verify).
Split-thickness grafts contract more and give a poorer functional and cosmetic result.

items.subject: Surgery
items.stem: A 40-year-old woman has stage IIB invasive ductal carcinoma that is estrogen receptor-negative, progesterone receptor-negative, and HER2-positive. What adjuvant systemic therapy is recommended?
options: Chemotherapy, trastuzumab, and an aromatase inhibitor
items.rationale: HER2-positive breast cancer is treated with anti-HER2 therapy: trastuzumab combined with chemotherapy substantially reduces recurrence and mortality and is continued for a year in the adjuvant setting, and pertuzumab may be added if lymph nodes are involved. Adjuvant endocrine therapy (tamoxifen or an aromatase inhibitor) is for estrogen receptor-positive disease.
expl: Trastuzumab is given in combination with chemotherapy, which substantially reduces recurrence and mortality.
Tamoxifen is endocrine therapy for estrogen receptor-positive disease; this tumor is receptor-negative.
Aromatase inhibitors are endocrine therapy for estrogen receptor-positive disease.

items.subject: Surgery
items.stem: Which neck dissection is used as a staging procedure for the clinically negative neck in oral cavity carcinoma?
items.rationale: Selective dissection of levels I to III (supraomohyoid neck dissection) is the procedure of choice for elective neck dissection in oral cavity cancer, and many surgeons use it as a staging procedure instead of sentinel node biopsy. Selective neck dissection is indicated when the risk of nodal disease exceeds 15% to 20%.

Central compartment dissection is used mainly for thyroid and laryngeal cancers (To verify).
Lateral neck dissection (levels II to IV) is used mainly for laryngeal and hypopharyngeal cancers (To verify).

items.stem: Which primary site of oral cavity squamous cell carcinoma has the best prognosis?
items.rationale: For localized cancer, 5-year survival exceeds 90% for the lip, exceeds 80% for the tongue, and is about 75% for the floor of the mouth. Metastases from lower lip cancers are rare; upper lip cancers tend to be more aggressive.
expl: Buccal mucosa cancer has a worse prognosis than lip cancer (To verify).
Localized tongue cancer has 5-year survival above 80%, lower than the lip.
Localized floor-of-mouth cancer has 5-year survival of about 75%.

items.stem: A bedridden patient has an area of nonblanchable redness over the sacrum with intact skin. What is the most important aspect of management?
options: Relief of pressure by regular repositioning
Incision and drainage of the area
items.rationale: Nonblanchable redness of intact skin over a bony prominence is a stage 1 pressure injury; an ulcer is not yet present but may form with continued pressure. Pressure reduction through regular repositioning, support surfaces, and less friction and moisture is the core of treatment, with direct wound care.
expl: Debridement removes eschar and necrotic tissue, which intact skin does not have.
There is no abscess to drain.
Antibiotics treat wound infection, which is absent here.

items.stem: Which feature is characteristic of a growing cancer?
options: Loss of the ability to invade adjacent tissue
New blood vessel growth induced by the tumor (angiogenesis)
items.rationale: As a cancer grows beyond what diffusion can supply, it releases angiogenesis factors such as vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) that promote formation of the new blood vessels needed for further growth. Local growth is aided by enzymes such as proteases that destroy adjacent tissue.
expl: Cancers stimulate new blood vessel growth rather than lacking vessels.
Cancers invade adjacent tissue with the help of enzymes such as proteases.
Cancers release angiogenesis factors that increase vascularity.

items.stem: What is the term for cytotoxic treatment given after curative resection of a tumor to lower the risk of recurrence?
items.rationale: Adjuvant therapy is additional cancer treatment given after the primary treatment to lower the risk that the cancer will recur. Neoadjuvant therapy is given before the primary treatment, usually before surgery, to shrink the tumor, and palliative care focuses on relief of symptoms.
expl: Palliative care focuses on relief of symptoms, pain, and stress in serious illness.
Neoadjuvant therapy is given before the primary treatment, usually before surgery.
Induction therapy is the first treatment given to achieve a response or remission (To verify).

items.subject: Surgery
items.stem: When are cancer cells considered invasive?
options: Once they have breached the basement membrane
When they overexpress tumor suppressor genes
Once angiogenesis gives them a growth advantage
Once they have gained replicative immortality
items.rationale: A neoplasm becomes invasive when its cells penetrate the basement membrane; for example, cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade 3 left untreated may penetrate the basement membrane and become invasive carcinoma. Tumors arise when tumor suppressor genes lose their function, and angiogenesis supports growth but does not define invasion.
expl: Tumors arise when tumor suppressor genes become unable to function, not when they are overexpressed.
Angiogenesis supplies a growing tumor but does not define invasion.
Replicative immortality supports tumor growth but does not define invasion (To verify).

items.subject: Surgery
items.stem: In a growing solid tumor, where are the most actively proliferating cancer cells found?
items.rationale: In larger tumor masses, a necrotic core is surrounded by a viable rim made of an inner layer of quiescent cells and an outer layer of proliferating cells; proliferating cells localize mainly to the outer rim. The core is poorly supplied with oxygen and nutrients (To verify).
expl: The center of a large tumor is necrotic.
The cells next to the necrotic core are quiescent.
Proliferation is concentrated in the outer rim, not spread evenly.

items.subject: Surgery
items.stem: What is the most common type of skin malignancy?
items.rationale: Basal cell carcinoma is the most common type of skin cancer, and the nodular subtype accounts for about 51% of basal cell carcinomas, followed by superficial (about 34%) and morpheaform or infiltrative (5% to 10%) types.
expl: Melanoma is much less common than basal cell carcinoma (To verify).
Squamous cell carcinoma is less common than basal cell carcinoma.
Morpheaform and infiltrative types make up only 5% to 10% of basal cell carcinomas.

items.rationale: Condylomata acuminata are benign anogenital warts most often caused by HPV types 6 and 11, and HPV is the most common sexually transmitted infection. Common and plantar warts are caused by HPV types that infect cutaneous epithelium and are not sexually transmitted (To verify).

expl: Size affects prognosis but ranks below histologic grade.
Sarcomas spread mainly to the lungs, and lymph node spread is less common (To verify).
Depth affects prognosis but ranks below histologic grade.

items.subject: Surgery
items.stem: Which change in a normal cell can lead to malignant transformation?
options: Deletion or inactivation of the p53 gene
Increased p53-mediated apoptosis of damaged cells
items.rationale: p53 prevents replication of damaged DNA in normal cells and promotes apoptosis of cells with abnormal DNA. Inactive or altered p53 lets cells with abnormal DNA survive and divide, error-prone DNA is passed to daughter cells, and neoplastic transformation results; TP53 is defective in many human cancers.
expl: Normal p53 protects against transformation by blocking replication of damaged DNA.
Apoptosis of cells with abnormal DNA is the protective action of normal p53.
Loss, not up-regulation, of E-cadherin is associated with tumor invasion (To verify).

items.stem: Which plain radiographic finding suggests that a bone tumor is malignant?
options: A lesion measuring 10% of the bone's length
A well-defined sclerotic border around the lesion
items.rationale: Radiographic features that suggest malignancy include an osteolytic destructive lesion, ill-defined permeative or moth-eaten bone loss, cortical destruction, soft-tissue extension, and pathologic fracture. A geographic lesion is sharply demarcated, whereas a permeative lesion has no clear border with normal bone.
expl: Size alone is not among the radiographic features listed as suggesting malignancy (To verify).
A sharply demarcated geographic margin is less suggestive of malignancy than an ill-defined permeative pattern.
A well-defined sclerotic border suggests a slow-growing, usually benign lesion (To verify).

items.stem: A 60-year-old man has right shoulder and upper back pain, paresthesia in the ulnar distribution of the right hand, right ptosis, and anhidrosis of the right face. Chest CT shows a 4-cm mass at the apex of the right lung with lysis of the posterior first and second ribs. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Cervical rib with thoracic outlet syndrome
items.rationale: Pancoast syndrome occurs when an apical lung tumor, usually non-small cell lung cancer, invades the brachial plexus, pleura, or ribs, causing shoulder and upper-extremity pain and hand weakness. items.stem: Which statement about intestinal obstruction is correct?
options: Repeated vomiting from small bowel obstruction usually causes hyperkalemia
Large-bowel obstruction causes vomiting earlier than small-bowel obstruction
Volvulus can cause strangulation, with infarction in as little as 6 hours
Bowel sounds are hypoactive early and hyperactive later in simple obstruction
items.rationale: Strangulating obstruction, with compromised blood flow, is usually associated with hernia, volvulus, or intussusception and can progress to infarction and gangrene in as little as 6 hours. In simple small-bowel obstruction, hyperactive, high-pitched peristalsis is typical, and a silent abdomen develops with infarction; repeated vomiting depletes sodium and potassium.
expl: Repeated vomiting depletes potassium rather than raising it.
Vomiting starts soon after small-bowel obstruction but is late and uncommon in large-bowel obstruction.
Peristalsis is hyperactive and high-pitched early and becomes silent with infarction.

items.stem: A direct impact or fall on a flexed wrist most likely causes which fracture?
items.rationale: Most distal radius fractures follow a fall on an outstretched hand and are dorsally displaced (Colles fractures); volar displacement, called Smith (reverse Colles) fracture, occurs when the wrist is flexed during the injury.

items.stem: A 35-year-old hairdresser has fever and a fusiform swelling of her right index finger, held slightly flexed, with tenderness along the volar surface and severe pain when the finger is passively extended. A few days earlier, a strand of hair cut her cuticle. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.rationale: Infectious flexor tenosynovitis, usually from penetration and bacterial inoculation of the flexor tendon sheath, causes the Kanavel signs: flexed resting position of the digit, fusiform swelling, tenderness along the flexor tendon sheath, and pain with passive extension. Treatment is surgical drainage and antibiotics.
expl: Overuse causes gradual pain without fever and lacks some Kanavel signs (To verify).
Trigger finger causes pain in the palm with catching of the digit, without fever or fusiform swelling (To verify the absence).
