items.stem: Which statement about antimicrobial stewardship is correct?
options: Restricted antimicrobials need no monitoring once they have been approved
A more expensive antimicrobial can be assumed to be more effective
It optimizes antimicrobial selection, dose, and duration to limit resistance
Its main goal is to increase the use of broad-spectrum antimicrobials
items.rationale: Antimicrobial stewardship is the optimal selection, dosing, and duration of antimicrobial treatment to achieve the best clinical outcome with minimal side effects and minimal impact on subsequent resistance. expl: Tracking antimicrobial use is a core element of stewardship programs.
The price of an antimicrobial does not indicate its effectiveness (To verify).
Stewardship promotes optimal, responsible use rather than broader use.

items.stem: Plain radiographs of a 70-year-old woman show generalized decreased bone density. What is required to diagnose osteoporosis?
options: The radiographic finding of decreased density alone

Radiographs can only suggest low bone density; it must be confirmed by bone densitometry.
Serum calcium is usually normal in osteoporosis (To verify).

items.rationale: The most common causes of massive hemoptysis, which vary by region, are bronchogenic carcinoma, bronchiectasis, and tuberculosis and other pneumonias. Aspergillomas are usually indolent and only occasionally cause hemoptysis, although bleeding can prompt resection.

A healed, calcified granuloma rarely bleeds (To verify).

items.stem: Which change after birth promotes constriction and closure of the ductus arteriosus?
options: A rise in carbon dioxide tension
A fall in arterial oxygen tension
items.rationale: At birth, the rise in PaO2 and the decline in prostaglandin concentration cause closure of the ductus arteriosus, typically beginning within the first 10 to 15 hours of life. Cyclooxygenase inhibitors such as indomethacin or ibuprofen are used to close a symptomatic patent ductus in preterm infants.
expl: A rise in carbon dioxide does not promote ductal closure (To verify).
A rise, not a fall, in PaO2 promotes closure.
Pulmonary fibrosis is unrelated to ductal closure (To verify).

options: Expiratory wheezing over the lung fields
A holosystolic murmur at the apex
A midsystolic click with a late murmur

items.subject: Surgery
items.stem: Which finding defines a type I (sliding) hiatal hernia?
options: The fundus has herniated beside the esophagus while the junction stays below the hiatus
The stomach and the colon have herniated into the chest
The junction and a large part of the stomach, including the fundus, are in the chest
The gastroesophageal junction and cardia alone have slid above the diaphragm
items.rationale: Type I (sliding) hernias, more than 95% of cases, have the gastroesophageal junction and part of the stomach above the diaphragm. In type II (paraesophageal), the fundus is in the mediastinum while the junction stays below the hiatus; type III combines both, with the junction and a variable portion of the stomach in the mediastinum; and type IV includes another organ such as the colon.
expl: This describes a type II (paraesophageal) hernia.
Herniation of another organ such as the colon defines a type IV hernia.
This describes a type III (mixed) hernia.

items.stem: A hypotensive patient has a low cardiac index, high systemic vascular resistance, low mixed venous oxygen saturation, and low central venous pressure. What type of shock is this?
items.rationale: Hypovolemic shock shows decreased filling pressures, decreased cardiac output, increased systemic vascular resistance, and decreased mixed venous oxygen saturation. Cardiogenic shock has the same pattern but with increased filling pressure (PCWP), and distributive shock, including septic and neurogenic shock, has increased cardiac output and decreased systemic vascular resistance.
expl: Neurogenic shock is a form of distributive shock with decreased systemic vascular resistance.
Cardiogenic shock has increased, not decreased, filling pressures.
Septic (distributive) shock has decreased systemic vascular resistance and increased cardiac output.

items.stem: A 63-year-old smoker becomes febrile and dyspneic 2 days after subtotal gastrectomy for gastric cancer. He has leukocytosis, and a chest x-ray shows new pulmonary infiltrates. What is the diagnosis?
items.rationale: Hospital-acquired pneumonia develops at least 48 hours after hospital admission and was not incubating at the time of admission. The most common pathogens are Staphylococcus aureus, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and other gram-negative bacilli.
expl: Pneumonia arising 48 hours or more after admission is hospital acquired.
New fever, leukocytosis, and infiltrates point to pneumonia rather than chronic lung disease (To verify).
A smoker's cough does not cause fever, leukocytosis, and new infiltrates (To verify).

items.stem: What is a goal of surgical repair of a hiatal hernia?
options: Leaving the hiatal defect open to avoid dysphagia
Enlarging the esophageal hiatus to lower pressure
Restoring an intra-abdominal segment of esophagus at least 2 cm long
Leaving the gastroesophageal junction in the chest
items.rationale: Repair has 3 key tenets: obtaining at least 2 cm of tension-free intra-abdominal esophageal length, closing the hiatus, and performing a fundoplication. The lower esophageal sphincter and the crural diaphragm together form the antireflux barrier.
expl: Hiatal closure is one of the key steps of repair.
The hiatus is closed, not enlarged.
The gastroesophageal junction is returned below the diaphragm.

items.stem: What is the usual cause of an acute hemolytic transfusion reaction from ABO incompatibility?
options: Antibodies against donor leukocyte HLA antigens
Clerical error in labeling or identification
Bacterial contamination of the blood unit
items.rationale: ABO incompatibility is the most common cause of an acute hemolytic transfusion reaction, itself the most common cause of transfusion-related death. It usually results from mislabeling the recipient's pretransfusion sample at collection or failing to match the intended recipient with the blood product immediately before transfusion. The most common transfusion complications overall are febrile nonhemolytic reactions.
expl: Antibodies to donor leukocyte HLA antigens cause febrile nonhemolytic reactions.
Overwarming damages red cells and causes hemolysis unrelated to ABO incompatibility.
Bacterial contamination causes septic reactions, not ABO-incompatible hemolysis (To verify).

items.stem: Using the 100/50/20 mL/kg/day rule, what is the daily maintenance fluid requirement of a 70-kg man after subtotal gastrectomy?
items.rationale: Maintenance fluid is 100 mL/kg for the first 10 kg, 50 mL/kg for each kg from 10 to 20 kg, and 20 mL/kg for each kg above 20 kg: 1,000 + 500 + (50 × 20) = 2,500 mL/day for 70 kg. This matches the adult water requirement of about 1 mL/kcal, or about 2,500 mL/day.
expl: 1,500 mL/day covers only the first 20 kg.
4,500 mL/day is nearly twice the requirement.
3,500 mL/day overestimates the requirement by 1,000 mL.

items.stem: A man has lost an estimated 1 L of blood from a scalp laceration that is now controlled. His heart rate is 110/min, and his systolic blood pressure is normal. What is the usual initial resuscitation fluid?
items.rationale: This patient has lost about 15% to 30% of his blood volume (a class 2 hemorrhage), with tachycardia but a normal systolic pressure. Initial management of hypovolemic shock is fluid resuscitation with a balanced isotonic crystalloid such as lactated Ringer's or normal saline. In major hemorrhage, blood products are given as soon as possible, and damage control resuscitation favors early blood products over large volumes of crystalloid.
expl: Whole blood is not the usual initial fluid for a controlled class 2 hemorrhage (To verify).
Albumin has shown little evidence of survival benefit over crystalloid.
Plasma is given with red cells in major hemorrhage, not as the initial fluid here.

items.stem: Which statement about surgical antibiotic prophylaxis is correct?
options: Redosing is required after the first hour of operating time
It is indicated for clean operations that place a prosthetic implant
The first dose is given immediately after the skin incision
The first dose is given after the wound is closed
items.rationale: Prophylactic antibiotics are standard when an artificial implant or foreign body is placed, in bone grafting, and in extensive operations with large expected blood loss. The first dose is given 30 to 60 minutes before the skin incision so that tissue levels peak during surgery, and a repeat dose is given when the operation lasts more than 4 hours or blood loss exceeds 1,500 mL.
expl: Redosing is needed for operations longer than 4 hours or blood loss above 1,500 mL.
The first dose is given 30 to 60 minutes before the incision.
A dose after closure cannot achieve peak tissue levels during surgery.

items.stem: Which acid-base disorder is most likely in hypovolemic shock from massive blood loss?
items.rationale: Type A lactic acidosis, the most serious form, occurs when lactic acid is overproduced in ischemic tissue during global hypoperfusion in hypovolemic, cardiogenic, or septic shock. Lactic acidosis is the most common cause of metabolic acidosis in hospitalized patients.

options: Routine antibiotic redosing at the second hour
Transfusion to keep hemoglobin above 10 g/dL

items.stem: What nourishes a skin graft during its first 48 hours?
items.rationale: A graft first passively absorbs oxygen and nutrients from the wound bed by imbibition and remains relatively ischemic. At about 48 hours, capillaries on the underside of the graft connect to vessels in the wound (inosculation), and further neovascularization follows as endothelial cells migrate into the graft.
expl: Revascularization by vessel ingrowth follows inosculation.
Inosculation, the connection of graft and bed capillaries, occurs at about 48 hours.
Vessel realignment is not the mechanism of early graft nutrition (To verify).

items.stem: After an attempted intubation, the patient can still make sounds, gurgling is heard over the epigastrium during ventilation, and oxygen saturation is falling. What is the appropriate management?
options: Leave the tube in place, since it is in the trachea
Remove the tube, oxygenate, and reattempt intubation
Advance the tube until breath sounds are equal
Withdraw the tube slightly until breath sounds are equal
items.rationale: Gurgling over the upper abdomen during ventilation indicates esophageal intubation, which, if unrecognized, causes failure to ventilate and hypoxic injury or death. When tracheal placement is in doubt, the tube is withdrawn and the patient ventilated with a facemask or supraglottic airway before another attempt. A patient who can still vocalize does not have a tube between the vocal cords (To verify).
expl: Gurgling over the epigastrium indicates esophageal, not tracheal, placement.
Advancing a tube that is in the esophagus does not place it in the trachea (To verify).
Withdrawing slightly corrects a mainstem bronchial intubation, not an esophageal one (To verify).

items.stem: A biopsy shows classic lobular carcinoma in situ (a noninvasive lesion of the lobules and terminal ducts) in the right breast. Which statement is correct?
options: She needs a right mastectomy with axillary node dissection
Imaging every 6 months for 3 years is the standard follow-up
She has an increased risk of invasive cancer in either breast
Her increased risk of invasive cancer is limited to the right breast

items.stem: A 70-year-old man comes to the emergency room after a nosebleed. His blood pressure is 200/100 mm Hg. The nose is full of clots, but there is no active bleeding. What is the next step?

items.stem: Which congenital anomaly of the airway or lung is the most likely to be fatal soon after birth?
items.rationale: Tracheal agenesis is a very rare anomaly with an estimated mortality of about 85%; only about 10 patients are known to have survived to 12 months, most after several operations. Bronchial atresia is usually an incidental finding with a favorable prognosis. Bilateral pulmonary agenesis or aplasia is fatal, but nearly all living patients with the condition have the unilateral form. Survival after repair of tracheoesophageal fistula exceeds 90% in pediatric surgical centers.

items.stem: A 7-year-old has fever and right lower quadrant pain that began a few days after an upper respiratory infection. Tenderness on palpation is milder than expected for appendicitis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.rationale: Mesenteric adenitis, inflammation of the mesenteric lymph nodes, causes right lower quadrant pain and is classically mistaken for acute appendicitis. It commonly follows a recent gastroenteritis or upper respiratory infection, and tenderness on palpation is notably less than in appendicitis. A child younger than 10 years with acute right lower quadrant pain is more likely to have mesenteric adenitis than appendicitis.

items.stem: Failure of the nasobuccal (oronasal) membrane to rupture during embryonic development causes which condition?
items.rationale: The nasobuccal membrane of Hochstetter normally ruptures after the sixth week to form the primitive nasal cavity with its choanae; its persistence is one proposed mechanism of choanal atresia. Because newborns are obligate nasal breathers, bilateral choanal atresia causes respiratory distress at birth, with cyanosis relieved by crying.
expl: Cleft lip results from failed fusion of the medial nasal process with the maxillary process.

Cleft palate results from failed midline fusion of the palatal shelves.

items.stem: A newborn has an abdominal wall defect with herniated bowel. Which finding indicates gastroschisis rather than omphalocele?
options: No membrane covers the herniated bowel
The infant has congenital heart disease
The herniated organs include the liver

items.stem: A Meckel diverticulum that contains ectopic gastric mucosa typically presents in a young child with which finding?
items.rationale: Acid secreted by ectopic gastric mucosa in the diverticulum ulcerates the adjacent ileum and causes bleeding, which is common in children younger than 11 years. Children classically have repeated episodes of painless, bright red rectal bleeding, usually not severe enough to cause shock. A Tc-99m pertechnetate scan identifies the ectopic gastric mucosa in 85% to 97% of bleeding children.
expl: Meckel diverticulitis causes pain typically localized below or adjacent to the umbilicus.
Distention comes with obstruction, most often from intussusception of the diverticulum.
Vomiting comes with obstruction, most often from intussusception of the diverticulum.

items.stem: What is the most common cause of acute pancreatitis?
items.rationale: Gallstones are the most common cause of acute pancreatitis (40% to 70% of cases): a stone that obstructs the ampulla of Vater causes gallstone pancreatitis. Alcohol is the second most common cause (25% to 35%). Hypertriglyceridemia accounts for about 1% to 4% of cases, and medications such as valproate are less common causes.
expl: Alcohol intake is the second most common cause.

items.subject: Surgery
items.stem: A patient has an elevated total bilirubin that is mostly unconjugated (indirect). Aminotransferase levels are normal, and there is no bilirubin in the urine. Which diagnosis is most consistent with these results?
items.rationale: Bilirubin is produced when hemoglobin is broken down into unconjugated bilirubin, so hemolysis raises the unconjugated fraction, with no bilirubin in the urine and normal aminotransferase levels. Viral hepatitis causes conjugated hyperbilirubinemia from hepatocellular dysfunction, with aminotransferases usually above 500 U/L. Common bile duct stones and bile duct tumors obstruct extrahepatic bile flow and raise conjugated bilirubin, which is excreted in urine.
expl: Viral hepatitis causes conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, with aminotransferases usually above 500 U/L.
A common bile duct stone causes extrahepatic cholestasis with conjugated hyperbilirubinemia.
A bile duct tumor obstructs extrahepatic bile flow and raises conjugated bilirubin.

items.subject: Surgery
items.stem: A 61-year-old woman will undergo elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy. If antibiotic prophylaxis is given, which agent is the usual choice?
items.rationale: For most surgical procedures, including abdominal surgery, a single parenteral dose of cefazolin is given shortly before surgery, ideally within 60 minutes before the incision. Vancomycin is added only for patients with documented MRSA colonization. Carbapenems such as meropenem have an extremely broad spectrum and are often the last resort for multidrug-resistant gram-negative organisms.

Vancomycin is added for patients with documented MRSA colonization.
Carbapenems are often the last resort for multidrug-resistant gram-negative organisms.

items.stem: A 62-year-old man with a known common bile duct stone develops right upper quadrant pain, jaundice, and fever with chills. Which complication has developed?
items.rationale: Bile duct stones cause biliary colic, biliary obstruction, gallstone pancreatitis, or cholangitis. Acute cholangitis is suspected in patients with abdominal pain, jaundice, and fever or chills; it is a surgical emergency that requires aggressive supportive care, antibiotics, and urgent stone removal and drainage, endoscopically or surgically.

Acute cholecystitis usually results from a stone obstructing the cystic duct.
Biliary colic occurs when the ducts become partially obstructed; fever further suggests cholangitis.

items.subject: Surgery
items.stem: A 55-year-old woman with obstructive jaundice from a common bile duct stone is scheduled for cholecystectomy and bile duct exploration. Her prothrombin time is prolonged. What should she receive before surgery?
items.rationale: Biliary obstruction causes fat malabsorption and vitamin K deficiency, which prolongs the prothrombin time (PT) and raises the INR. When fat malabsorption is the cause or bleeding risk is high, vitamin K (phytonadione) is given parenterally; if IV phytonadione shortens the PT within 2 to 6 hours, vitamin K deficiency rather than liver disease is the cause. Untreated, bleeding may begin as an ooze from a surgical incision.
expl: Vitamin A has no role in clotting factor synthesis (To verify).
Heparin is an anticoagulant and would increase bleeding (To verify).
Warfarin is a coumarin anticoagulant that antagonizes vitamin K.

items.subject: Surgery
items.stem: As liver synthetic function declines, which coagulation abnormality usually appears first?
items.rationale: All coagulation factors are made in the liver, so both the prothrombin time (PT) and partial thromboplastin time (PTT) are prolonged in severe liver disease. Factor VII has the shortest plasma half-life and falls first, so the PT is prolonged earliest in incipient liver disease. An isolated prolonged PTT with a normal PT suggests hemophilia A or B, and thrombocytopenia accompanies splenomegaly in advanced portal hypertension.
expl: A prolonged PTT with a normal PT and platelet count suggests hemophilia A or B.
Liver disease lowers the platelet count; thrombocytopenia accompanies splenomegaly in portal hypertension.
Fibrinogen abnormalities contribute to clotting disturbances in many patients but are not the earliest change (To verify).

items.stem: In acute pancreatitis, what is the Grey Turner sign?

items.subject: Surgery
items.stem: Which imaging study is preferred to assess acute pancreatitis for local complications such as necrosis?
items.rationale: CT with IV contrast is the imaging study of choice to establish the diagnosis of acute pancreatitis when it is uncertain and to assess for local complications; necrosis is best seen on contrast-enhanced cross-sectional imaging. Abdominal ultrasound is done when gallstone pancreatitis is suspected, to detect gallstones or a dilated common bile duct, but overlying gas frequently obscures the pancreas. Plain radiographs may show calcifications within the pancreatic ducts but do not assess necrosis.

PET has no role in evaluating acute pancreatitis (To verify).
Ultrasound looks for gallstones and bile duct dilation; overlying gas frequently obscures the pancreas.

items.subject: Surgery
items.stem: A 69-year-old man has obstructive voiding symptoms. His International Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS) is 20, and his quality-of-life score is 5. The prostate is smooth, firm, nontender, and about 28 g. Urinalysis is normal, and the prostate-specific antigen (PSA) level is 3.8 ng/mL. He has had no urinary retention, infection, or stones. What is the appropriate initial management?
items.rationale: An IPSS of 20 indicates severe symptoms. Initial treatment of uncomplicated obstructive symptoms from benign prostatic hyperplasia is a trial of medication; alpha-adrenergic blockers such as tamsulosin decrease voiding problems. Surgery such as transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP) is done when patients do not respond to medication or develop complications such as recurrent urinary tract infection, calculi, severe bladder dysfunction, or upper tract dilation.
expl: Surgery is done when medication fails or complications develop; he has neither.
5-alpha reductase inhibitors shrink the prostate over months and help mainly glands larger than 30 mL; this gland is about 28 g.
A PSA above 4 ng/mL prompts shared decision-making about further tests or biopsy; this PSA is 3.8 ng/mL.

Dysuria suggests infection, which can complicate obstruction, and nocturia can follow polyuria from impaired kidney concentrating ability.

items.stem: When the carbohydrate supply falls, which tissue can most readily switch to fatty acids and ketone bodies for energy?
items.rationale: Most tissues can oxidize fatty acids, and cardiac and skeletal muscle take up ketone bodies for ATP generation, so muscle is the least affected by a fall in carbohydrate supply. Red blood cells and the lens lack mitochondria and depend entirely or almost entirely on glycolysis. The brain is primarily dependent on glucose and uses ketone bodies only during sustained fasting.
expl: The brain is primarily dependent on glucose and uses ketone bodies only during sustained fasting.
Red blood cells lack mitochondria; glycolysis to lactate is their sole source of ATP.
The lens lacks mitochondria and relies entirely or almost entirely on anaerobic glycolysis.

items.rationale: About 9 L of water enter the gastrointestinal tract daily; the small intestine absorbs 7 to 8 L, and the colon absorbs the remaining 1 to 2 L. Together they absorb 99% of the fluid load, so even a small reduction in absorption can cause diarrhea.

items.subject: Surgery
items.stem: A 13-year-old boy has sudden left scrotal pain and swelling. Color Doppler ultrasound shows an enlarged left testis with decreased to absent blood flow. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.rationale: Testicular torsion is rotation of the testis that strangulates its blood supply. It is most common between ages 12 and 18 years and more common on the left, presents with severe, sudden scrotal pain and swelling, and is confirmed by color Doppler ultrasound. Testicular salvage falls from 80% to 100% at 6 to 8 hours to near zero at 12 hours.
expl: A varicocele is a painless mass that becomes smaller when the patient lies down.
An epididymal cyst (spermatocele) is a painless cystic mass that transilluminates.
Orchitis, usually viral, causes inflammation and does not cut off testicular blood flow (To verify the flow finding).

items.stem: A patient with a stab wound to the chest is hypotensive, with jugular venous distention, muffled heart sounds, and a paradoxical pulse. Which hemodynamic profile is expected?
options: Low wedge pressure, high cardiac output, low vascular resistance
High wedge pressure, high cardiac output, low vascular resistance
Low wedge pressure, low cardiac output, high vascular resistance
High wedge pressure, low cardiac output, high vascular resistance
items.rationale: Jugular venous distention, muffled heart sounds, and a paradoxical pulse suggest cardiac tamponade, a cause of obstructive shock, in which mechanical factors interfere with filling of the heart. In tamponade, the pulmonary capillary wedge pressure is increased, cardiac output is decreased, and systemic vascular resistance is increased. Hypovolemic shock has a decreased wedge pressure with low output and high resistance; distributive shock has a decreased wedge pressure, high output, and low resistance.
expl: This is the profile of distributive shock.
A high wedge pressure with high output and low resistance is not a classic shock profile (To verify).
This is the profile of hypovolemic shock.

items.stem: Which finding is an indication for elective repair of an asymptomatic abdominal aortic aneurysm in a woman?

items.rationale: Peripheral nodular enhancement with progressive fill-in is the typical pattern of a hemangioma. Hemangiomas are usually small and asymptomatic and occur in up to 20% of adults; biopsy is usually not necessary, and treatment is usually not indicated. Resection is considered only for troublesome symptoms or rapid enlargement.

items.stem: A 30-year-old man who injects drugs is diagnosed with a pyogenic liver abscess. Which organism must empiric antibiotics cover, given his risk factor?
items.rationale: Pyogenic liver abscesses are usually polymicrobial (E. coli, Klebsiella, streptococci, staphylococci, and anaerobes), but hematogenous spread, as from endocarditis, can seed the liver. Staphylococcus aureus bacteremia, which frequently causes metastatic foci of infection, is particularly common among people who inject drugs, so empiric therapy must cover S. aureus.
expl: Tuberculosis is a rare cause of liver abscess (To verify).
Entamoeba histolytica causes amebic, not pyogenic, liver abscess.
Pseudomonas is not among the usual organisms of pyogenic liver abscess (To verify).

items.subject: Surgery
items.stem: Which anterior mediastinal mass is primarily treated with chemotherapy and radiation rather than surgical resection?
items.rationale: Most malignant mediastinal tumors are removed surgically, but lymphomas are best treated with chemotherapy, with radiation as consolidation. Surgical resection is the primary, potentially curative treatment for thymoma, whose most common paraneoplastic syndrome is myasthenia gravis. Teratomas are usually benign and are resected when symptomatic, and substernal goiter is usually managed by resection to relieve symptoms, prevent complications, and confirm the diagnosis.
expl: Substernal goiter is usually managed by surgical resection.
Teratomas are resected when they become symptomatic.
Surgical resection is the primary treatment for thymoma.

items.stem: A 43-year-old man has a right anterior neck mass that has enlarged over 5 years, with progressive hoarseness and dyspnea when lying supine. He has no palpitations, tremor, or weight change. The 4 × 6 cm mass is smooth, not hard, and moves with swallowing, and there is no cervical lymphadenopathy. Along with a TSH level, which study should be ordered first?
options: CT scan of the neck and mediastinum
items.rationale: A mass that moves with swallowing is thyroid in origin. Initial evaluation of a thyroid nodule includes history, examination, TSH, and thyroid ultrasonography to characterize the nodule; the decision to perform fine-needle aspiration, preferably ultrasound-guided, is based on risk stratification that includes the ultrasound findings. CT and MRI evaluate extrathyroidal extension, not the nodule itself.

CT evaluates extrathyroidal extension, not the nodule itself; it may follow to define retrosternal extension (To verify).
The decision to perform fine-needle aspiration follows risk stratification that includes the ultrasound findings.

items.subject: Surgery
items.stem: Which complication can follow surgery in a patient whose hyperthyroidism was not adequately controlled before the operation?
items.rationale: Thyroid storm is an acute form of hyperthyroidism that results from untreated or inadequately treated severe hyperthyroidism and may be precipitated by surgery, infection, or trauma. It causes fever, marked weakness, restlessness, confusion, vomiting, diarrhea, and tachycardia or cardiovascular collapse, and is a life-threatening emergency. Hypocalcemia from hypoparathyroidism and hypothyroidism can follow thyroid surgery whether or not hyperthyroidism was controlled.
expl: Hypoparathyroidism with hypocalcemia is a complication of thyroid surgery itself.
Hypothyroidism follows total thyroidectomy whether or not hyperthyroidism was controlled (To verify).
Wound infection is not specific to uncontrolled hyperthyroidism (To verify).

items.subject: Surgery
items.stem: Which thyroid cancer is diagnosed histologically by capsular and vascular invasion?
items.rationale: Follicular thyroid carcinoma is diagnosed by follicular cells that lack the nuclear atypia of papillary cancer, together with capsular and vascular invasion; follicular adenoma is benign and more common. Follicular carcinoma spreads hematogenously. Papillary carcinoma is recognized by its nuclear features (Orphan Annie eye nuclei) and psammoma bodies and invades lymphatics.
expl: Papillary carcinoma is recognized by its nuclear features and psammoma bodies.
Anaplastic carcinoma is an undifferentiated cancer.
Medullary carcinoma arises from parafollicular cells that produce calcitonin.

items.subject: Surgery
items.stem: Which incidentally discovered adrenal mass can be managed without surgery?
options: A functioning 1-cm adenoma with hormone excess
A nonfunctioning 5-cm mass with indeterminate imaging features
A functioning 5-cm adenoma with hormone excess
A nonfunctioning 3-cm mass with benign imaging features
items.rationale: An incidental adrenal mass is assessed for hormone excess and for imaging features of malignancy. The risk of adrenocortical carcinoma rises with size (about 2% below 4 cm, 6% at 4.1 to 6 cm, and 25% above 6 cm); an indeterminate nodule larger than 4 cm should be offered surgery, whereas a lesion with benign features under 4 cm needs no further imaging. A functioning adenoma with clinically significant hormone excess is offered adrenalectomy regardless of size. An unenhanced CT attenuation of 10 HU or less indicates a lipid-rich benign adenoma.
expl: A functioning adenoma with clinically significant hormone excess is offered adrenalectomy regardless of size.
An indeterminate nodule larger than 4 cm should be offered surgery.
A functioning adenoma with clinically significant hormone excess is offered adrenalectomy.

items.subject: Surgery
items.stem: Which type of selective neck dissection is most commonly performed for thyroid cancer?
items.rationale: Selective neck dissection removes the nodal levels at risk based on patterns of cervical spread. The thyroid drains to level VI, the central compartment, which contains the thyroid and parathyroid glands; oral cavity cancers drain to levels I to III, and laryngeal and pharyngeal cancers to levels II to IV. Prophylactic central-compartment dissection is considered in node-negative papillary carcinoma with advanced primary tumors (T3 or T4).
expl: Levels I to III are the drainage of oral cavity cancers.
Posterolateral dissection is used for cancers of the posterior scalp and neck (To verify).
Levels II to IV are the drainage of laryngeal and pharyngeal cancers.

items.stem: A 50-year-old man has a 5-cm papillary thyroid carcinoma confined to the thyroid, and his cervical lymph nodes are clinically negative. What is the surgical treatment of choice?
options: Total thyroidectomy with lateral (modified radical) neck dissection
items.rationale: For papillary carcinoma larger than 4 cm, the initial operation should be a near-total or total thyroidectomy; lobectomy is an option only for unifocal tumors smaller than 4 cm without extrathyroidal extension or nodal metastasis. Lateral neck dissection is not done for clinically node-negative disease, although prophylactic central-compartment dissection may be considered for advanced primary tumors (T3 or T4).

Subtotal thyroidectomy leaves thyroid tissue; tumors larger than 4 cm need near-total or total thyroidectomy.
Lateral neck dissection treats clinically involved lateral nodes; these nodes are clinically negative (To verify).

items.subject: Surgery
items.stem: A 66-year-old man has blood-tinged nasal mucus, a left level II neck mass, and fullness in the left ear. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.rationale: Nasopharyngeal cancer often presents with palpable neck node metastases. Hearing loss from eustachian tube obstruction with a middle ear effusion is another common presenting symptom, along with bloody rhinorrhea or epistaxis. The nasopharynx is examined with a mirror or endoscope and biopsied; open cervical node biopsy should not be the first procedure.
expl: Nasal polyps cause nasal obstruction without a metastatic neck mass (To verify).
An antrochoanal polyp causes nasal obstruction without a metastatic neck mass (To verify).
Adenoid hypertrophy causes nasal obstruction, mainly in children, without a metastatic neck mass (To verify).

items.stem: An 18-year-old woman has throat pain and difficulty speaking. One side of the soft palate is swollen, and the uvula is displaced to the opposite side. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.rationale: Peritonsillar abscess, most common in adolescents and young adults, causes severe unilateral sore throat, trismus, a muffled "hot potato" voice, and deviation of the uvula away from the swollen tonsillar area.

Chronic pharyngitis does not cause unilateral palatal swelling with uvular deviation (To verify).
Diphtheria produces a dirty gray, tough, adherent pharyngeal exudate.

items.subject: Surgery
items.stem: In children, where does an ingested foreign body most commonly become impacted?
items.rationale: The esophagus is the most common site of foreign body impaction, at its physiologic narrowings: the upper esophageal sphincter (the cricopharyngeus, at C6), the aortic arch (T4), and the lower esophageal sphincter. About 74% of pediatric foreign bodies impact at the upper esophageal sphincter, whereas about 68% of adult impactions occur in the distal esophagus.
expl: Most adult impactions occur in the distal esophagus; in children most occur at the upper esophageal sphincter.
The piriform sinus is a pharyngeal site; most pediatric impactions occur at the upper esophageal sphincter.
The vallecula is a pharyngeal site; most pediatric impactions occur at the upper esophageal sphincter.

items.subject: Surgery
items.stem: A 5-year-old boy is brought to the emergency room after a suspected coin ingestion. He is stable and has no respiratory distress. What is the initial management?
options: Chest and neck radiographs, including a lateral view
Discharge with instructions to return if distress develops
Examination of the oropharynx with an attempt to extract the coin
Back blows or the Heimlich maneuver
items.rationale: Plain radiographs are first-line imaging for a suspected esophageal or gastric foreign body, and two views are preferred. The lateral view separates a button battery, which shows a 2-layer appearance, from a coin, which appears as a single-layer disk; an impacted disk battery may cause esophageal burns, perforation, or a tracheoesophageal fistula.
expl: An impacted esophageal coin or battery must be located before any decision to observe (To verify).
Blind attempts at extraction come before the object is located (To verify).
Back blows and the Heimlich maneuver are for airway obstruction; this child is breathing comfortably (To verify).

items.subject: Surgery
items.stem: Which statement about the management of caustic ingestion is correct?
options: An alkali such as sodium hydroxide should be neutralized with an acid
Endoscopy is generally done within 24 hours of ingestion
Corticosteroids are given when perforation is likely
Oral or pharyngeal burns reliably show whether the esophagus is burned
items.rationale: Endoscopy does not need to be immediate, but the consensus is to perform it within 24 hours, after the patient is stabilized; it may be safe up to 96 hours with gentle insufflation, and later endoscopy risks perforating friable tissue. Neutralizing an alkali with an acid (or vice versa) is contraindicated. The presence or absence of intraoral burns does not reliably indicate esophageal or gastric burns. IV corticosteroids are not recommended, and perforation is treated with antibiotics and surgery.
expl: Neutralizing a caustic with an acid or alkali is contraindicated.
IV corticosteroids are not recommended; perforation is treated with antibiotics and surgery.
The presence or absence of intraoral burns does not reliably indicate esophageal injury.

items.subject: Surgery
items.stem: Which thyroid carcinoma has the most favorable survival despite its tendency to spread to lymph nodes?
items.rationale: Papillary carcinoma, 80% to 90% of thyroid cancers, invades lymphatics, yet papillary and follicular cancers have an overall 5-year survival of 98.4%. Follicular carcinoma is more aggressive because it spreads hematogenously; patients with metastatic medullary carcinoma generally die of their cancer; and anaplastic carcinoma has high mortality.
expl: Follicular carcinoma is more aggressive than papillary carcinoma because it spreads hematogenously.
Mortality is high for anaplastic thyroid cancer.
Patients with metastatic medullary carcinoma may live for years but generally die of their cancer.

items.subject: Surgery
items.stem: Which single thyroid function test gives the most information about thyroid function?
items.rationale: TSH measurement is the best means of determining thyroid dysfunction: a normal TSH excludes hyperthyroidism and hypothyroidism except in central (pituitary or hypothalamic) disease or rare pituitary resistance to thyroid hormone. Changes in TSH with normal T4 and T3 define subclinical hyperthyroidism and hypothyroidism.
expl: A normal total T4 does not exclude subclinical thyroid disease, which TSH detects.
A normal free T4 does not exclude subclinical thyroid disease, which TSH detects.
T3 is measured in selected cases, such as suspected T3 toxicosis (To verify).

items.stem: A 50-year-old man has a 1.5-cm pleomorphic adenoma in the superficial lobe of the right parotid gland. What is the best management?
items.rationale: Pleomorphic adenoma, the most common benign salivary gland tumor, has an incomplete pseudocapsule with microscopic tumor extensions, so simple enucleation has recurrence rates of 15% to 45%. Superficial lobe tumors smaller than 3 cm are optimally treated by superficial parotidectomy with facial nerve preservation, with recurrence below 2%. Untreated tumors grow and risk malignant transformation; total parotidectomy is for deep lobe tumors or superficial tumors larger than 4 cm.

Untreated tumors grow progressively and risk malignant transformation.
Total parotidectomy is for deep lobe tumors or superficial lobe tumors larger than 4 cm.

items.stem: What is the most common bacterial cause of acute tonsillopharyngitis in children?
items.rationale: Tonsillopharyngitis is usually viral; in about 30% of patients the cause is bacterial, and group A beta-hemolytic streptococcus (GABHS) is the most common bacterial cause. GABHS causes about 15% to 30% of sore throats in children and occurs most often between ages 5 and 15. Diphtheria and gonorrhea are rare causes.
expl: Gonorrhea is a rare cause of tonsillopharyngitis.
Diphtheria is a rare cause of tonsillopharyngitis.
Neisseria meningitidis is not a usual cause of tonsillopharyngitis (To verify).

items.subject: Surgery
items.stem: A 6-year-old boy has fever, difficulty swallowing, and throat pain that began this morning. He is drooling and leans forward with his chin thrust out to breathe. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.rationale: Epiglottitis is a rapidly progressive bacterial infection of the epiglottis and surrounding tissues that may cause sudden airway obstruction. In children, sore throat, odynophagia, and dysphagia develop abruptly; drooling without a barking cough is a hallmark, and fatal asphyxia may occur within hours. Since Hib vaccination, it has become rare in children.
expl: Bronchopneumonia does not cause drooling and dysphagia (To verify).
In tonsillopharyngitis the tonsils are swollen and red, without abrupt airway compromise (To verify the second part).
An esophageal foreign body causes dysphagia and drooling but not fever with airway posturing (To verify).

items.stem: A 25-year-old medical student is hit over the right ear by a water balloon, and water enters the ear canal. Otoscopy shows a slitlike perforation of the right tympanic membrane. What is the best initial management?
options: Antibiotic ear drops with dry ear precautions
Dry ear precautions alone, without antibiotics
Insertion of a tympanostomy tube through the perforation
items.rationale: Most traumatic perforations heal spontaneously, and dry ear precautions are recommended. Routine antibiotic drops are unnecessary, but prophylactic antibiotic drops are needed when contaminants such as water may have entered through the perforation, because purulent otorrhea may begin within 24 to 48 hours. Surgery is reserved for perforations persisting more than 2 months.
expl: Perforations are not sutured; those persisting more than 2 months are repaired surgically (To verify the first part).
Dry ear precautions alone suit a clean perforation; water has entered this ear.
A tympanostomy tube is not a treatment for a traumatic perforation (To verify).

items.stem: Which graft material is most commonly used to repair a tympanic membrane perforation?
items.rationale: Autologous grafts for tympanoplasty are usually temporalis fascia or tragal or conchal perichondrium. Temporalis fascia is used more commonly than cartilage, with success rates of 93% to 97%; cartilage, which resists shrinkage, is chosen when more stability is needed, as in recurrent or high-risk perforations.
expl: Muscle is not used as a tympanic membrane graft (To verify).
A fat graft is not the standard graft for tympanoplasty (To verify).
Cartilage is used for recurrent or high-risk perforations; temporalis fascia is used more often.

items.stem: What is the most common type of facial nerve paralysis?
items.rationale: Facial nerve palsy is often idiopathic (formerly called Bell palsy): a sudden, unilateral peripheral palsy affecting the upper and lower face, presumed to result from swelling of the nerve from an immune or viral process, most often herpes simplex virus. expl: HIV is a less common cause than idiopathic palsy (To verify).
Trauma is a less common cause than idiopathic palsy (To verify).

items.stem: When oral antibiotics are prescribed for a patient with nasal packing, which organism are they mainly intended to cover?
items.rationale: Nasal packing can become a nidus for infection, including sinusitis and toxic shock syndrome; nasal packing is a risk factor for toxic shock syndrome, which is most commonly caused by a toxigenic strain of Staphylococcus aureus. Prophylactic antibiotics are at the clinician's discretion and are not standard practice, because there is no strong evidence that they prevent sinusitis or toxic shock syndrome.
expl: Moraxella catarrhalis is a cause of bacterial sinusitis, not the main target of packing prophylaxis.
Haemophilus influenzae is a cause of bacterial sinusitis, not the main target of packing prophylaxis.
Pneumococci cause bacterial sinusitis, not toxic shock syndrome from packing (To verify the second part).

items.subject: Surgery
items.stem: A 35-year-old man has nasal congestion and watery rhinorrhea whenever he is exposed to perfume. He has little itching or sneezing, and allergy testing is negative. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.rationale: Vasomotor rhinitis, the most common form of nonallergic rhinitis, is a chronic condition in which intermittent vascular engorgement of the nasal mucosa causes watery rhinorrhea and congestion. Sensory nerve endings in the nasal mucosa respond to chemical irritants, temperature changes, and strong odors such as perfume; sneezing and itching are less common than other nasal symptoms.
expl: Acute rhinosinusitis does not recur with each exposure to an odor (To verify).
Allergy testing is negative, and itching and sneezing are minimal.
Rhinitis medicamentosa follows prolonged use of topical decongestants (To verify).

items.subject: Surgery
items.stem: CT is the criterion standard for imaging the paranasal sinuses. What makes it so valuable?
options: It gives the best soft-tissue contrast
It defines the sinus anatomy and drainage pathways
It distinguishes viral from bacterial infection
It is needed to diagnose uncomplicated acute sinusitis
items.rationale: CT is the criterion standard for sinus imaging: it shows opacification and mucosal thickening, assesses ostial obstruction such as at the osteomeatal complex, detects bony erosion, assesses the orbits and cribriform plates, and is used for surgical planning and image-guided procedures. Acute sinusitis is diagnosed clinically, with CT only when complications are suspected; MRI gives the best soft-tissue contrast and complements CT.
expl: MRI gives the best soft-tissue contrast; CT complements it.
CT does not identify the infecting organism (To verify).
Imaging is not indicated in acute sinusitis unless complications are suspected.

items.stem: A maxillary sinus cancer involves the infraorbital nerve. Which symptom is it most likely to cause?
items.rationale: Paranasal sinus cancer occurs most often in the maxillary and ethmoid sinuses and causes symptoms late, from pressure on adjacent structures: pain, nasal obstruction and discharge, epistaxis, diplopia, ear fullness, facial paresthesias, and loosening of the maxillary teeth below the sinus. Loose maxillary teeth reflect invasion of the floor of the sinus, not the infraorbital nerve (To verify).
Facial asymmetry reflects tumor bulk, not nerve involvement (To verify).

items.rationale: The intrinsic laryngeal muscles are the thyroarytenoid, lateral cricoarytenoid, posterior cricoarytenoid, cricothyroid, and interarytenoid; all except the posterior cricoarytenoid adduct the vocal folds, and abduction results from posterior cricoarytenoid activation. items.stem: A 50-year-old man accidentally swallowed muriatic (hydrochloric) acid. How should he be managed?
options: Esophagoscopy within 24 hours if a burn is suspected
Barium swallow to assess the extent of injury
items.rationale: Because the presence or absence of intraoral burns does not reliably show whether the esophagus and stomach are burned, endoscopy is done when the history or symptoms suggest more than a trivial ingestion; the consensus is within 24 hours, once the patient is stable. If perforation is suspected, CT of the chest and abdomen is done, and perforation is treated with antibiotics and surgery; IV corticosteroids are not recommended.

Surgery is for perforation or full-thickness injury, not a routine first step (To verify).
IV corticosteroids are not recommended; perforation is treated with antibiotics and surgery.

items.stem: In head and neck squamous cell carcinoma, which nodal levels does a lateral (selective) neck dissection remove?
options: Levels I, II, III, and IV
Levels II, III, IV, and V
items.rationale: A selective (lateral) neck dissection removes levels II to IV, the nodes that drain the larynx, hypopharynx, and oropharynx. Oral cavity cancers drain to levels I to III, and a modified radical neck dissection removes levels I to V. In papillary thyroid cancer, a lateral dissection usually includes levels IIa, III, IV, and Vb.
expl: Adding level I extends the dissection to the oral cavity drainage (To verify).
Level V is included in a modified radical dissection, and in lateral dissection for thyroid cancer.
Levels I to III are the drainage of oral cavity cancers.

items.subject: Surgery
items.stem: Idiopathic facial nerve (Bell) palsy is thought to result from swelling of the nerve, which becomes compressed and ischemic in its bony canal. What is the mainstay of treatment?
items.rationale: The presumed mechanism is swelling of the facial nerve from an immune or viral disorder; the swollen nerve is compressed in the labyrinthine portion of the facial canal, causing ischemia and paresis. Glucocorticoids, ideally begun within 3 days of onset, give faster and more complete recovery; antiviral drugs against herpes simplex add no benefit. The cornea must be protected from drying.
expl: Supplements are not a treatment for Bell palsy (To verify).
Vasodilators are not a treatment for Bell palsy (To verify).
NSAIDs do not reduce nerve swelling the way glucocorticoids do (To verify).

items.stem: A patient stands upright with the feet together and the eyes closed while the examiner watches for 30 seconds for swaying or loss of balance. What is this test?
items.rationale: In the Romberg test, the patient stands with the feet together, first with the eyes open and then closed. The test is positive if the patient can stand with the eyes open but sways or falls once vision is removed, which indicates impaired proprioception from the posterior (dorsal) columns.
expl: Vestibulospinal reflexes maintain posture but are not a named bedside test (To verify).
The vestibulo-ocular reflex stabilizes gaze during head movement (To verify).
The Moro reflex is an infant startle reflex (To verify).

items.stem: A woman has hearing loss, tinnitus, and vertigo after 1 week of an untreated upper respiratory tract infection. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.rationale: Labyrinthitis, inflammation of the membranous labyrinth of the inner ear, causes vertigo, nausea, vomiting, tinnitus, and hearing loss, and its most common cause is a viral upper respiratory tract infection. Vestibular neuritis is confined to the vestibular nerve and spares hearing. Meniere disease causes recurrent episodes with fluctuating low-frequency hearing loss.

Acute otitis media causes ear pain and conductive hearing loss rather than vertigo (To verify).
Meniere disease causes recurrent episodes with fluctuating low-frequency hearing loss.

Deferring evaluation would miss HIV infection (To verify).

items.stem: Your uncle, who has diabetes, has had blurred vision in his right eye for a few days. Ophthalmoscopy of his left eye shows red and white patches scattered over the retina, but the right eye has no red-orange reflex. What should you suspect in the right eye?
items.rationale: In proliferative diabetic retinopathy, new vessels grow into the vitreous and can bleed, and vitreous hemorrhage is usually due to this cause; it is painless and causes floaters, haze, or shadows. An absent red reflex can indicate vitreous hemorrhage, and the fellow eye's hemorrhages and exudates show diabetic retinopathy. A large cataract can also obliterate the red reflex, but it develops gradually (To verify the time course).
expl: Retinal detachment causes floaters, flashes, and a curtain over the field (To verify its effect on the red reflex).
Anterior uveitis causes ocular ache, photophobia, and ciliary flush.
A large cataract can obliterate the red reflex but does not appear over a few days (To verify the time course).

items.subject: Surgery
items.stem: On routine funduscopy, a 57-year-old woman without diabetes has retinal hemorrhages, discrete pale yellow dots (hard exudates), and fluffy white patches (cotton-wool spots). Using the Wong and Mitchell classification, what do these findings indicate?
options: Moderate retinopathy with a strong association with stroke
Normal age-related changes needing no follow-up
Mild retinopathy with no association with stroke
items.rationale: In the Wong and Mitchell classification, retinal hemorrhages, microaneurysms, cotton-wool spots, and hard exudates define moderate hypertensive retinopathy, which is strongly associated with clinical and subclinical stroke, cognitive decline, and cardiovascular death. Mild retinopathy (arteriolar narrowing, arteriovenous nicking) has only a modest association, and malignant retinopathy adds optic disc swelling. Treatment is directed at controlling blood pressure.
expl: Hemorrhages, exudates, and cotton-wool spots are not age-related changes (To verify).
Mild retinopathy consists of arteriolar narrowing and nicking and still carries a modest association with stroke.
Malignant retinopathy requires optic disc swelling, which is absent.

items.stem: A 32-year-old woman has sudden blurred vision in the right eye with pain that worsens on eye movement. Right visual acuity is 20/200, with a right relative afferent pupillary defect, abnormal color vision, and a normal fundus. Where is the lesion?
items.rationale: A relative afferent pupillary defect points to the optic nerve or the retina. With a normal fundus and color vision disturbed out of proportion to acuity, the lesion is in the optic nerve behind the globe; in about two-thirds of optic neuritis cases the inflammation is entirely retrobulbar, with no visible change in the optic nerve head.
expl: Vitreous disease does not cause an afferent pupillary defect with a normal fundus view (To verify).
Corneal disease does not cause an afferent pupillary defect (To verify).
Retinal disease severe enough to cause an afferent defect would be visible on funduscopy (To verify).

items.stem: A 32-year-old woman has sudden blurred vision in the right eye with pain that worsens on eye movement. Right visual acuity is 20/200, with a right relative afferent pupillary defect, abnormal color vision, and a normal fundus. Which test should be ordered to confirm the diagnosis?
options: MRI of the brain and orbits
items.rationale: Gadolinium-enhanced MRI of the brain and orbits is recommended for young patients with eye pain on movement and vision loss or an afferent pupillary defect. It confirms optic neuritis, usually showing enhancement of the optic nerve, and helps diagnose multiple sclerosis, MOG antibody-associated disease, and neuromyelitis optica.
expl: Optical coherence tomography images the retina, which is normal here (To verify).
Fluorescein angiography images the retinal circulation, which is normal here (To verify).
A chest radiograph does not show the optic nerve (To verify).

items.stem: A 25-year-old badminton player was hit in the left eye by a shuttlecock 2 hours ago. He had pain, tearing, floaters, flashes of light (photopsia), and photophobia. items.rationale: Dark floaters and flashes of light (photopsias) are early symptoms of retinal detachment, followed by a curtain or veil across the field of vision; ocular trauma is a cause. A corneal injury does not cause a visual field defect (To verify).

options: Direct ophthalmoscopy through an undilated pupil
Gonioscopy of the anterior chamber angle

The slit lamp examines the anterior segment and anterior vitreous.

items.subject: Surgery
items.stem: Which of these conditions is a true ophthalmologic emergency?
items.rationale: Central retinal artery occlusion causes sudden, painless, monocular vision loss; retinal infarction can occur as quickly as 90 minutes after the occlusion, after which vision loss is permanent, so immediate treatment is indicated to lower intraocular pressure and dislodge the embolus. Central retinal vein occlusion is treated with anti-VEGF medications and other measures for its complications, and subconjunctival hemorrhage resolves on its own.
expl: Central retinal vein occlusion is treated for its complications, such as macular edema, rather than emergently (To verify the timing).
Retinoblastoma needs prompt cancer care but is not a minutes-to-hours emergency (To verify).
Subconjunctival hemorrhages are absorbed spontaneously within 1 to 3 weeks.

items.subject: Surgery
items.stem: What is the most important initial management of a chemical burn of the eye?
items.rationale: Caustic chemical burns of the eye are a medical emergency: irrigation should begin as soon as possible, even on site with tap water before medical help arrives, and continue for at least 30 minutes. A drop of anesthetic may be used but must not delay irrigation, and topical anesthetics are avoided afterward; mild burns are later treated with topical antibiotics.
expl: Analgesia does not limit the chemical injury (To verify).
An anesthetic drop may be given but must not delay irrigation, and topical anesthetics are avoided afterward.
Topical antibiotics are used later for mild burns, after irrigation.

items.stem: Where is the blockage most often located in congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction?
items.rationale: The nasolacrimal duct opens into the inferior meatus through a mucosal flap called the valve of Hasner, and the most common cause of congenital obstruction is persistence of a membrane at the distal end of the duct at that valve. items.rationale: The canaliculi lie at the medial margins of the eyelids, so medial eyelid lacerations may involve them. Canalicular lacerations may not be obvious on examination; probing, or injecting fluorescein or air into the opposite punctum to see it emerge from the cut canaliculus, helps make the diagnosis. items.stem: A 54-year-old man who has had diabetes for 15 years has gradually blurring vision and, over a few days, hair-like floaters that grew denser until he could not recognize faces. After the basic eye examination, what is the next step?
items.rationale: Diabetic retinopathy is diagnosed by funduscopy; all patients with type 2 diabetes need an annual dilated eye examination, and visual symptoms such as blurred vision are indications for ophthalmologic referral. items.subject: Surgery
items.stem: Most of an instilled eye drop is lost before it can be absorbed. What is the main reason?
items.rationale: Tear turnover accounts for most drug loss. An eyedropper delivers about 39 µL on average, but the eye holds only about 30 µL, so the excess is lost through nasolacrimal drainage and reflex blinking; instillation also triggers reflex tearing, which speeds the loss. Larger drops therefore do not increase absorption, and faster tear flow reduces it.
expl: Mucin binding is not the main route of drug loss (To verify).
Corneal metabolism is not the main route of drug loss (To verify).
Evaporation is not the main route of drug loss (To verify).

items.subject: Surgery
items.stem: Which statement about topical ophthalmic preparations is true?
options: Eye drops reach high concentrations in the vitreous
Gels are hydrophobic and commonly blur vision
Ointments prolong contact time, allowing less frequent dosing
Ointments are easy to apply and rarely blur vision
items.rationale: Ointments slow elimination of the drug by tear flow and prolong corneal residence time, increasing bioavailability, but they blur vision, so they are often advised at night. Gels are made of hydrophilic polymers and also prolong residence time. Conventional eye drops have limited bioavailability because of precorneal clearance.
expl: Conventional eye drops have limited bioavailability because of precorneal clearance.
Gels are usually made of hydrophilic polymers.
Ointments are responsible for blurred vision.
